name: Cycladic folded-arm figurine
museum: Museum of Cycladic Art, Athens; and worldwide

claims.text: Cycladic figurines were carved from marble using abrasive techniques.
They were originally painted, with pigment traces still detectable.
The canonical type was made to lie flat, consistent with burial use.
Most examples in collections lack archaeological context due to looting.
They represent a mother goddess or fertility deity.
Many surviving figurines show evidence of deliberate ancient breakage, particularly at the neck, possibly as part of funerary ritual.

milestones.text: Christos Tsountas excavates Early Cycladic cemeteries, including Chalandriani on Syros, giving figurines their first recorded contexts.
Modernist taste for their pure forms fuels a collecting boom and widespread looting of Cycladic graves; most known figurines have no recorded findspot.

summary: Slender marble figures with folded arms and blank faces — abstract to modern eyes, and originally brightly painted.
significance: The signature art of the Early Bronze Age Cyclades — and a lesson in how looting erases meaning, since most known figurines have no recorded findspot.
body:
Marble figurines made in the Cycladic islands of the Aegean around 2800–2300 BC, during the Early Bronze Age. The classic type is a standing nude woman, a few centimetres to over a metre tall, with arms folded right under left across the stomach, and a flat, tilted-back face with only a ridge for a nose. They were shaped with emery, a hard abrasive found on Naxos, and polished with pumice.

Today they look white and abstract, but they were painted. Traces of red and blue pigment survive, and "paint ghosts" — differences in weathering — show where eyes, hair and patterned markings once were. Most cannot stand: their feet point downward, so they were made to lie flat, which fits their usual findspot in graves. Many were broken in antiquity, sometimes deliberately at the neck, perhaps as part of funeral rites. Whether they represent goddesses, ancestors, servants or the dead themselves is unknown.

The first excavated examples with known contexts came from Christos Tsountas's work in Cycladic cemeteries such as Chalandriani on Syros in 1898–99. In the 20th century their simple forms appealed to modern artists such as Brancusi, Modigliani and Henry Moore. The resulting collectors' market drove massive looting of graves, and forgeries entered collections; most figurines now in museums have no recorded archaeological context.

name: The Keros Harp Player

claims.text: Cycladic marble figures depict seated musicians with harps.
They are the earliest known depictions of musicians in European art.
The Keros deposit contains figurine fragments broken elsewhere and brought there.
Keros functioned as a regional ritual centre.

milestones.text: Reported as found in a grave on Keros with a flute player; the find was not witnessed by the scholar who announced it.

summary: A seated marble figure playing a harp — the earliest depiction of a musician in European art.
significance: The earliest image of a musician in European art, showing that stringed instruments were played in the Aegean almost 5,000 years ago.
body:
A marble figurine of a seated man playing a frame harp, about 22 cm tall, made in the Cyclades around 2800–2300 BC. It was reported in 1884 as found in a grave on the small island of Keros, together with a double-flute player, though the find was not properly recorded. Both are in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

About a dozen seated musicians are known from the Cyclades, almost all harpists. They are more fully three-dimensional than the standard folded-arm figurines, with a convincing seated posture on a backed chair. The harp is carved with a distinct soundbox, a curved neck and a crossbar holding the strings, detailed enough for musical historians to reconstruct how such an instrument was built.

The figures prove that music with stringed instruments existed in the Aegean by the early 3rd millennium BC. Whether they show gods, performers at funerals or the dead themselves is unknown.

Keros itself has become central to understanding Cycladic religion. Excavations there have found a "Special Deposit" of thousands of broken figurines and vessels, broken elsewhere and brought to the island, suggesting it was a ritual centre for the region — perhaps the earliest such place in the Aegean.

name: The Phaistos Disc

claims.text: The disc bears 241 sign impressions using 45 distinct symbols.
The signs were made with individual reusable stamps.
The text remains undeciphered.
It records a language rather than a decorative or numerical scheme.
The disc is a modern forgery.

milestones.text: Found by Luigi Pernier in a storeroom of the palace at Phaistos, alongside a Linear A tablet.

summary: A clay disc stamped with 241 signs in a spiral, made with reusable punches — and completely undeciphered.
significance: The earliest known use of stamped, movable type, and one of the most famous undeciphered texts in the world.
body:
A disc of fired clay about 16 cm across, made on Crete around 1700–1600 BC. It was found in 1908 by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier in a storeroom of the Minoan palace at Phaistos, alongside a Linear A tablet, and is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

Both faces carry 241 impressions of 45 different signs — heads with plumed crowns, figures, ships, shields, plants — arranged in a spiral and divided by lines into 61 groups that probably represent words. The signs were not drawn but pressed into the wet clay with individually carved stamps. That makes the disc the earliest known example of movable type, around three thousand years before printing in Europe.

It cannot be read. Deciphering an unknown script needs either a bilingual text or a large body of inscriptions, and the disc offers neither: no other text in its script has been found. Dozens of proposed decipherments have been published, and none is accepted. Its uniqueness has led some to suspect a forgery, but most specialists reject this, since it was found in a recorded excavation.

Whether its script is Cretan or came from elsewhere in the Aegean or Anatolia is also unknown.

name: The Bull-Leaping Fresco

claims.text: Minoan art repeatedly depicts humans vaulting over bulls.
The surviving fresco is heavily reconstructed from small fragments.
Skin colour conventions in the fresco distinguish male and female figures.
The specific manoeuvre shown was physically performed.

milestones.text: Fragments found by Arthur Evans in the Court of the Stone Spout, in the palace's east wing.
Émile Gilliéron reconstructs the panel from the largest pieces; the painting seen today is largely his reconstruction.

summary: Three figures and a charging bull — the defining image of Minoan Crete, and heavily restored.
significance: The defining image of Minoan Crete — and a reminder of how much of that image is modern reconstruction.
body:
A painted plaster wall panel about 80 cm high from the palace at Knossos, made around 1550–1450 BC. Arthur Evans found its fragments in 1901 in the palace's east wing, and the restorer Émile Gilliéron reconstructed the panel. It is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

A charging bull fills the panel. One figure vaults over its back, another grips its horns and a third waits behind it, arms outstretched. By the conventions of Aegean and Egyptian art, darker skin marks men and paler skin women, so the scene seems to show both taking part. It probably belonged to a series of bull-leaping panels.

Bull-leaping appears again and again in Minoan art, on seal stones, gold rings and bronzes, so some form of sport or ritual with bulls clearly played a major part in Minoan life. Whether the exact leap shown here — seizing the horns and somersaulting over the back — could actually be performed has been argued for a century.

Much of what is seen today is restoration. Only fragments survived, and Gilliéron filled the gaps to produce the complete, confident image reproduced everywhere. It shows the Bronze Age through an early 20th-century lens, as much as it records it.

name: The Snake Goddess

claims.text: Faience figurines of women holding snakes were found in the Knossos Temple Repositories.
The figurines were restored from incomplete fragments with modern additions.
Several comparable "Minoan" figurines elsewhere are modern forgeries.
The figures represent a snake goddess.

milestones.text: Found by Arthur Evans in the stone-lined Temple Repositories at Knossos, in pieces and restored for display.

summary: A faience figurine of a bare-breasted woman holding snakes — the most reproduced Minoan image, and among the least secure.
significance: The most reproduced image of Minoan religion — and one of the least secure, shaped as much by its restorers as by its makers.
body:
A faience figurine about 34 cm tall, made on Crete around 1650–1550 BC. Arthur Evans found it in 1903 with a second, smaller figure in the stone-lined "Temple Repositories" at Knossos, among broken ritual objects. Both are in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

The figure wears a long flounced skirt and an open bodice that leaves the breasts bare. Snakes coil around her arms and up to her head. The smaller figure holds a snake in each raised hand.

Much of the familiar image is restoration. The smaller figure was missing its head and one arm; the head, the hat and the small cat on top were added from separate fragments or invented. "Snake Goddess" is Evans's interpretation: the figures could be goddesses, priestesses or worshippers. Snakes appear with female figures on other Minoan objects, so some link between snakes and women's religious roles is likely, but its meaning is unknown.

The figure's fame created a market. In the early 20th century convincing forgeries of Minoan "goddesses" in ivory and gold entered major museum collections, and several famous examples are now regarded as fakes.

name: The Harvester Vase

claims.text: The Harvester Vase depicts a procession of about 27 figures carrying agricultural tools.
One figure shakes an Egyptian-type sistrum, indicating cultural contact.
The scene depicts singing during collective labour.
The procession is agricultural rather than military.

milestones.text: Found by the Italian School of Archaeology, under Federico Halbherr and Luigi Pernier, in the villa at Hagia Triada.

summary: A carved stone rhyton showing a procession of singing workers — the liveliest crowd scene in Aegean art.
significance: The liveliest crowd scene in Aegean art, and the earliest known image of people singing as they work.
body:
A carved stone ritual vessel (rhyton) of black steatite, made on Crete around 1500–1450 BC. It was found in 1902 by the Italian School of Archaeology at the villa of Hagia Triada, near Phaistos, and is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. Only the upper part survives.

A band of relief shows a procession of about 27 men marching with long-handled tools — winnowing forks or hoes — over their shoulders, led by a man in a scaled cloak. In the middle, a group of four sing, led by a man shaking a sistrum, an Egyptian rattle. Their open mouths and straining chests are carved with unusual realism, and one marcher has stumbled and is being jostled by the man behind.

The tools point to an agricultural festival, perhaps for harvest or sowing, though some read the scene as a military or religious procession. The sistrum is a sign of Minoan contact with Egypt.

The vessel is a high point of Minoan stone carving. Its sense of movement, crowding and individual behaviour has no parallel in the more formal art of contemporary Egypt or the Near East.

name: Marine Style octopus flask

claims.text: This Marine Style flask was found at Palaikastro and dates to c. 1500–1450 BC.
Its painted decoration comprises large octopuses together with sea urchins, triton shells, rocks and seaweed.
The decoration is composed to follow and cover the vessel's three-dimensional form.
The vessel is attributed to the Marine Style Master, to whom a closely related stirrup jar from Gournia is also attributed.
The terracotta flask stands approximately 27 centimetres high.

summary: A 27-centimetre terracotta flask from Palaikastro, its surface filled by octopuses and seabed motifs — an iconic work of Minoan Marine Style.
significance: The best-known example of Minoan Marine Style, the pottery in which sea creatures were made to fill and follow the shape of the vessel.
body:
This painted terracotta flask was found at Palaikastro on the eastern coast of Crete and dates to approximately 1500–1450 BC, during the Minoan New Palace period. Now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, it stands about 27 centimetres high. Its rounded body and paired handles provide a continuous surface on which the marine composition unfolds.

Large octopuses dominate the decoration. Although their bodies face the viewer, they appear to swim diagonally, while their tentacles extend, curl and overlap across the vessel's curved surface. Smaller sea urchins, triton shells, rocks and seaweed occupy the spaces between them. This dense arrangement—sometimes described by the art-historical term *horror vacui*, or fear of empty space—makes the pot itself seem like an underwater environment rather than a neutral support for a flat picture.

The vessel belongs to the Marine Style, a distinctive phase of Late Minoan pottery in which sea life was adapted closely to the shapes of ceramic vessels. The imagery reflects the importance and familiarity of the sea to communities on Crete, but its precise meaning and the flask's original use cannot be established from the decoration alone. It is therefore safer to read the design as evidence for artistic observation and ceramic practice than as proof of a particular religious symbolism.

The museum attributes the flask to the so-called Marine Style Master. A closely related stirrup jar from Gournia—with similar octopus imagery—is attributed to the same painter. That comparison suggests shared artistic practice across eastern Crete, although the surviving objects do not reveal exactly how the painter or workshop was organised.

name: The Hagia Triada Sarcophagus

claims.text: The sarcophagus depicts a bull sacrifice with blood collected in a vessel.
One scene shows offerings brought to a figure before a tomb.
It combines Minoan and Mycenaean religious iconography.
The standing figure represents the deceased receiving cult.

milestones.text: Found by Roberto Paribeni in Tomb 4 of the hilltop cemetery at Hagia Triada.

summary: The only painted limestone sarcophagus from Bronze Age Crete, and the fullest surviving image of Aegean funerary ritual.
significance: The fullest picture of Bronze Age Aegean funeral ritual, painted at the moment Minoan and Mycenaean traditions were merging on Crete.
body:
A limestone coffin 1.37 m long, coated in plaster and painted on all four sides, made on Crete around 1400–1370 BC. It was found in 1903 by Roberto Paribeni in a tomb near the villa at Hagia Triada, in southern Crete, and is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum. It is the only Minoan sarcophagus painted in this way.

On one long side, a bull lies trussed on a table with its blood draining into a vessel, while a woman makes an offering at an altar to the music of a double pipe. On the other, women pour liquid into a large bowl set between double axes topped by birds, while men carry a model boat and young animals towards a figure standing before a building — probably the dead man at his tomb, receiving offerings.

It was made after the Mycenaean Greeks took control of Knossos, and shows the two cultures combined: Minoan double axes, dress and painting style, with a Mycenaean-style emphasis on honouring the dead. Most of what is known of Aegean funeral ritual from images rather than bones comes from this single object.

The richness of the tomb and its closeness to the grand buildings at Hagia Triada suggest it was made for someone of high local rank.

name: The Malia Bee Pendant

secondaryImage.caption: The Aegina Treasure, now in the British Museum -- almost certainly looted from the same Chrysolakkos cemetery in the 1890s and falsely sold as coming from the island of Aegina, decades before the site was ever formally excavated.

claims.text: The pendant was found at the Chrysolakkos complex at Malia.
It demonstrates granulation, filigree and repoussé techniques.
Linear B tablets record honey as an offering to deities.
The insects depicted are bees rather than wasps.
The British Museum's "Aegina Treasure" was looted from Chrysolakkos in the 1890s and given a false provenance.

milestones.text: Found by the French School at Athens in the Chrysolakkos burial complex at Malia, and published by Pierre Demargne.

summary: Two bees holding a honeycomb between them, in gold — a technical showpiece of Minoan metalwork.
significance: The finest piece of jewellery to survive from Bronze Age Crete, and a showcase of Minoan goldsmiths' mastery of granulation.
body:
A gold pendant 4.6 cm across, made on Crete around 1800–1700 BC. It was found in 1930 by the French School at Athens in Chrysolakkos, the elite burial complex of the palace town of Malia on Crete's north coast, and is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

Two insects face each other, their curved bodies meeting around a granulated disc — perhaps a drop of honey or a honeycomb. Their wings are made of fine wire, three small discs hang below, and a tiny cage above may once have held something. The goldsmith combined three demanding techniques: repoussé (hammering the sheet from behind), filigree (fine soldered wire) and granulation (fusing tiny gold beads to the surface without visible solder). Minoan craftsmen had mastered granulation by about 2000 BC; after the palace age it vanished from the Aegean for centuries.

The insects are usually called bees, though some argue their narrow waists suggest a wasp. Bees mattered: honey was the only concentrated sweetener, and later Linear B tablets record honey offered to the gods.

Chrysolakkos — "the pit of gold" — was robbed by local diggers from the 1880s. The British Museum's "Aegina Treasure", bought in 1892, is widely thought to have been looted from it. The pendant survived because it was found in a recorded excavation.

name: The Zakros Rock Crystal Rhyton

secondaryImage.caption: The remote Minoan palace site at Kato Zakros, on Crete's east coast -- destroyed and never resettled or looted, which is why its shrine treasury was still standing when Nikolaos Platon's team reached it in the 1960s.

claims.text: The rhyton was carved from rock crystal and reassembled from over 300 fragments.
It was recovered from the intact treasury at Zakros.
Its manufacture required advanced abrasive stone-working technique.
The vessel's handle survived almost intact, made of rock-crystal beads still threaded on their original bronze wire.

milestones.text: Found in the treasury of the unlooted palace at Zakros during Nikolaos Platon's excavations, and restored from hundreds of fragments.

summary: A libation vessel of carved rock crystal, reassembled from over 300 fragments — the finest surviving Minoan stone vessel.
significance: The finest stone vessel to survive from Minoan Crete, and a product of the only Minoan palace found unlooted.
body:
A ritual pouring vessel (rhyton) carved from a single block of rock crystal, about 16 cm high, made on Crete around 1500–1450 BC. It was found by Nikolaos Platon's excavations, begun in 1961, in the treasury of the palace at Zakros on Crete's far eastern coast. Crushed into more than 300 fragments when the palace collapsed, it was reassembled and is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

Rock crystal is a very hard, transparent quartz that could not be cut with bronze tools. The vessel had to be ground into shape with abrasives such as emery, using drills and rubbing tools, with no way to correct a mistake. Its body is left plain to show off the stone. The neck ring is made of gilded faience, and the handle is a row of crystal beads threaded on bronze wire, found still in its original order.

Zakros, with a good harbour facing Egypt and the Levant, was the smallest of Crete's major palaces. Destroyed around 1450 BC, it was never resettled or robbed, so its shrine treasury was found almost as its owners left it, filled with vessels of stone. A second famous rhyton from the same palace, of green chlorite, is carved with a picture of a mountain sanctuary.

name: The Akrotiri frescoes
museum: Museum of Prehistoric Thera; National Archaeological Museum, Athens

claims.text: The Akrotiri frescoes were preserved in situ by volcanic ash.
The miniature frieze depicts a fleet, coastal towns and armed men.
The Saffron Gatherers depicts a ritual involving a seated female figure.
The frescoes depict specific historical events.
No human remains have been found among the ruins, supporting the view that Akrotiri's population evacuated before the final eruption.

milestones.text: Spyridon Marinatos begins excavating the town buried by the Thera eruption; the frescoes are found still on their walls.

summary: Wall paintings preserved by volcanic ash, including a miniature frieze of a fleet passing between two towns.
significance: The best-preserved wall paintings of the Bronze Age Aegean, giving a fuller picture of daily life, ships and ritual than anything surviving on Crete.
body:
Wall paintings from the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri on the island of Thera (Santorini), painted around 1650–1600 BC. They were buried in place by ash from the great Theran eruption and have been excavated since 1967, first by Spyridon Marinatos and then by Christos Doumas. They are displayed in the Museum of Prehistoric Thera and the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Because the ash preserved whole rooms, the paintings can be seen in their original settings. The miniature "Flotilla" frieze, several metres long, shows a fleet of ships with rowers and cabins sailing between coastal towns, watched by people on rooftops, with dolphins in the sea. It also shows drowned men and warriors in boar's-tusk helmets — not the entirely peaceful world once imagined for the Minoans. The "Saffron Gatherers" shows young women picking crocus and offering it to a seated goddess attended by a monkey and a griffin. Other panels show boxing boys, a fisherman carrying his catch, swallows among lilies and antelopes.

The style is closely related to Minoan painting on Crete, but the scenes show a prosperous island town with its own character.

No bodies have been found at Akrotiri, which suggests the inhabitants had warning and left before the final eruption.

name: The Mask of Agamemnon

claims.text: The mask was excavated by Schliemann at Mycenae in 1876 from Shaft Grave V.
It dates to c. 1550–1500 BC, centuries before any traditional Trojan War date.
It differs stylistically from the other masks in the same grave circle.
It depicts Agamemnon.
The mask was modified or forged in the 19th century.

milestones.text: Found by Heinrich Schliemann over a man's face in Shaft Grave V, Grave Circle A, Mycenae.
Claims that the mask was altered or forged are publicised; most specialists reject them.

summary: A hammered gold funerary mask from Mycenae Grave Circle A — misnamed, misdated, and unforgettable.
significance: The most famous object of the Greek Bronze Age, and the emblem of the gold-rich warrior elite whose burials mark the rise of Mycenae.
body:
A funeral mask of hammered gold, about 25 cm tall, made around 1550–1500 BC. Heinrich Schliemann found it in 1876 lying over the face of a man buried in Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A, inside the citadel of Mycenae. It is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

The mask was beaten from a single sheet of gold and its details chased into the surface. It shows a man with a narrow face, a full beard and a moustache, and closed eyes with the eyelids drawn over them. Five gold masks came from the shaft graves, and this one looks noticeably different from the rest.

Schliemann announced that he had found the tombs of Agamemnon and his companions; the famous line that he had "gazed on the face of Agamemnon" is probably a later embellishment. The burials are some three centuries older than any date for a Trojan War, so the identification is certainly wrong, but the name has stuck. The shaft graves, with their gold, weapons and imports, actually record the rise of the first Mycenaean ruling families.

In the 1970s–90s the classicist William Calder and the historian David Traill argued that the mask's unusual features showed it had been altered or faked in the 19th century. Most specialists reject this: the finds were witnessed and drawn at the time, and the technique fits Bronze Age goldwork.

name: Linear B tablet

claims.text: Linear B tablets record administrative inventories in early Greek.
They survive only because destruction fires baked the unfired clay.
The tablets name deities later worshipped in Classical Greece.
Tablet PY Ta 641 confirmed the decipherment of Linear B.
No literary or narrative texts in Linear B have been found.

milestones.text: Arthur Evans finds thousands of tablets at Knossos.
Carl Blegen finds the palace archive at Pylos, proving the script was used on the Greek mainland.
Michael Ventris shows the tablets are written in an early form of Greek.

summary: Unfired clay tablets recording palace inventories — accidentally preserved by the fires that destroyed the palaces.
significance: The earliest written Greek, and the only direct record of how a Mycenaean palace ran its economy and its gods.
body:
Clay tablets inscribed in Linear B, the script of the Mycenaean palaces, dating from about 1400 to 1180 BC. Thousands have been found, above all at Knossos on Crete (from 1900) and Pylos in Messenia (from 1939), with smaller groups from Mycenae, Thebes, Tiryns and elsewhere. Michael Ventris showed in 1952 that they record an early form of Greek. They are held mainly in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens, and the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

The tablets were never meant to last. They were unfired clay notes, kept for a season and then reused. They survive only where the fires that destroyed the palaces baked them hard.

Their content is entirely administrative: sheep counted by flock and shepherd, wool owed to the palace, bronze issued to smiths, chariot wheels checked, and rations for women textile workers and their children. There is no literature, history or law. But they also record offerings to gods later worshipped in Classical Greece — Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Athena, Hermes and Dionysus — and to a "Mistress of the Labyrinth" at Knossos. Scholars can even tell individual scribes apart by their handwriting.

One tablet from Pylos, PY Ta 641, confirmed the decipherment: it spells the Greek word for "tripods" next to drawings of three-legged pots.

name: The Dendra Panoply

claims.text: The Dendra panoply is the only complete Aegean Bronze Age body armour known.
The associated helmet is made from split boar tusks.
Homer describes boar's-tusk helmet construction accurately.
Experimental trials support its practical use in combat.

milestones.text: Found by Nikolaos Verdelis and Paul Åström in Chamber Tomb 12 at Dendra, a tomb already partly plundered.

summary: The only complete suit of Bronze Age body armour from the Aegean — fifteen bronze plates and a boar's-tusk helmet.
significance: The only complete suit of Bronze Age armour from the Aegean, and a direct link between the Mycenaean world and objects Homer still remembered.
body:
A suit of bronze body armour with a boar's-tusk helmet, made around 1450–1400 BC. It was found in 1960 by Nikolaos Verdelis and Paul Åström in Chamber Tomb 12 of the Mycenaean cemetery at Dendra, near Mycenae in the Argolid, and is now in the Archaeological Museum of Nafplio.

Fifteen hammered bronze plates, worn over a leather lining, form a cuirass with shoulder guards, a high collar and hanging plates protecting the hips and thighs. The helmet is made of split boar's tusks sewn onto a leather cap. Homer describes exactly this kind of helmet in the *Iliad*, centuries after it had gone out of use.

The armour weighs about 18 kg and restricts the arms, so it was long thought to be purely ceremonial or suitable only for a chariot fighter. In 2024 researchers had trained volunteers wear a replica through an eleven-hour simulated day of Bronze Age combat; they completed it, suggesting the suit was genuinely usable in battle.

Fragments of similar bronze plates from other Mycenaean sites show the Dendra suit was not unique, only the one that survived complete. It belongs to the world of chariot-riding warrior elites that ruled the Mycenaean palaces.

name: The Lion Gate

claims.text: The Lion Gate relief has stood in place at Mycenae since c. 1250 BC.
The relieving triangle is a structural device to protect the lintel.
The animals' heads were made separately and are lost.
The central column had religious significance.
The gate remained visible and known throughout antiquity, and later Greek travellers such as Pausanias described it directly.

milestones.text: Pausanias describes the lions over the gate; the relief has never been buried and stands where it was built.
Kyriakos Pittakis of the Archaeological Society at Athens clears the gateway.
Heinrich Schliemann excavates inside the gate, finding Grave Circle A.

summary: Two lionesses flanking a column above the main gate of Mycenae — the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe, still in place.
significance: The oldest monumental sculpture in Europe still standing where it was built, and the emblem of Mycenaean power.
body:
The main entrance to the citadel of Mycenae in the Argolid, built around 1250 BC as part of an extension of the fortification walls. It is still in place.

The gate is formed of huge stone blocks: two uprights and a lintel weighing around 20 tonnes. Above the lintel, the masonry leaves a triangular gap to take the weight off it, and this "relieving triangle" is filled with a limestone slab carved in relief. Two lionesses, or perhaps other beasts, stand facing each other with their forepaws on altars, flanking a single column. Their heads, made separately, are lost. Animals guarding a sacred symbol is a convention of Minoan and Near Eastern art, and the column was almost certainly a religious emblem as well as a sign of royal power.

Unlike most of the Mycenaean world, the gate was never buried or forgotten. The traveller Pausanias described it in the 2nd century AD and repeated the belief that Mycenae's massive walls were built by the giant Cyclopes. Kyriakos Pittakis cleared the gateway for the Archaeological Society at Athens in 1841, and in 1876 Heinrich Schliemann excavated just inside it, finding the gold-rich shaft graves of Grave Circle A.

name: The Vaphio Cups

claims.text: The Vaphio Cups were found in a Mycenaean tholos tomb in Laconia.
They depict contrasting scenes of capturing bulls by force and by decoy.
They were made using repoussé over a separate inner lining.
The cups are Minoan rather than Mycenaean products.

milestones.text: Found by Christos Tsountas in an unlooted cist inside a tholos tomb at Vapheio, near Sparta.

summary: A pair of gold cups showing bulls being captured — one violently, one gently — from a tholos tomb near Sparta.
significance: Masterpieces of Aegean goldwork, showing how closely Minoan art and Mycenaean wealth were entangled by 1500 BC.
body:
A pair of gold cups, each about 8 cm high, made around 1500–1450 BC. They were found in 1889 by Christos Tsountas in an unlooted pit inside a tholos (beehive) tomb at Vapheio, near Sparta, and are now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Each cup was hammered in relief (repoussé) from a single gold sheet and fitted with a smooth inner lining. Their scenes form a deliberate pair. On one, a bull charges into a net while another tosses two hunters into the air — capture by force. On the other, a bull is lured with a decoy cow and led away with a rope tied to its leg, while others graze — capture by cunning.

The style, with its lively animals and landscape, is Minoan, but the cups were found in a mainland Mycenaean tomb. Whether they were made on Crete and exported, made by Cretan craftsmen working on the mainland, or made by Mycenaean artists copying Minoan style has been debated since their discovery.

The tomb also held other rich offerings, marking the burial of a powerful local ruler in Laconia at a time when mainland elites were acquiring Minoan luxury goods and adopting Minoan art.

name: The Warrior Vase

claims.text: The Warrior Vase depicts a file of uniformly equipped Mycenaean soldiers.
It dates to the final phase of the Mycenaean palace period.
The equipment differs markedly from earlier elaborate armour like the Dendra panoply.
The female figure is making a gesture of farewell or mourning.

milestones.text: Found by Heinrich Schliemann in a house just inside the citadel at Mycenae.

summary: A krater showing a file of armoured soldiers marching out, with a woman raising her hand behind them.
significance: The best-known image of Mycenaean soldiers, painted as the palace world was collapsing around them.
body:
A painted pottery krater (mixing bowl) about 41 cm high, made around 1200–1150 BC. Heinrich Schliemann found it in 1876 in a house just inside the citadel walls at Mycenae — since called the House of the Warrior Vase — and it is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

On the main side six soldiers march in step, wearing horned helmets, corselets and greaves and carrying round shields and spears with small bags tied below the points, perhaps rations for the march. At the far left a woman raises her hand, in a gesture usually read as farewell or mourning. On the other side another file of soldiers marches the opposite way.

The vase belongs to the very end of the palace period, when Mycenaean citadels were strengthening their walls and then being destroyed. The soldiers' equipment is lighter and more uniform than the elaborate Dendra armour of two centuries earlier, closer to the gear of later infantry. It suggests a society shifting from individual aristocratic display to standardised troops under pressure.

Who the soldiers were marching against, and whether the scene records a real departure, cannot be known; but it captures the anxious last years of Mycenae.

name: The Pylos Combat Agate

claims.text: The Pylos Combat Agate was excavated in 2015 from an unlooted Mycenaean grave.
Details on the sealstone measure well under a millimetre.
No magnifying devices are attested from the Bronze Age Aegean.
Its anatomical naturalism is unmatched until the Classical period.

milestones.text: Found by Jack Davis and Sharon Stocker in the unlooted Griffin Warrior grave at Pylos, encrusted with limestone.
Cleaning reveals the miniature combat scene, and the find is announced.

summary: A sealstone 3.6 cm wide carved with a combat scene whose detail is invisible to the naked eye.
significance: A carving of astonishing skill that forced archaeologists to rethink what Bronze Age Aegean artists could do, a thousand years before Classical sculpture.
body:
A carved agate sealstone 3.6 cm long, made around 1450 BC, probably on Crete. It was found in 2015 by Jack Davis and Sharon Stocker in the unlooted grave of the "Griffin Warrior" near the palace of Pylos in Messenia, and is now in the Archaeological Museum of Chora.

Encrusted with limestone, it was not recognised until it was cleaned and its carving announced in 2017. It shows a battle: a warrior plunges his sword into the neck of an opponent, while a third man lies dead at their feet. The bodies are carved with detailed muscles, and the weapons and jewellery are shown precisely, some details less than half a millimetre across — too small to see clearly without magnification, though no magnifying lenses are known from the Bronze Age Aegean.

Such anatomical realism in a human figure in motion is not matched in Greek art until the Classical period, a thousand years later. The find undermines the idea that Greek naturalism grew steadily out of simple Geometric beginnings.

The Griffin Warrior's grave held more than a thousand objects, combining mainland weapons with Minoan gold rings and seals — evidence that Minoan art and luxury goods were prized by the Mycenaean elite before Mycenae's rise.

name: The Medinet Habu reliefs

claims.text: The reliefs depict land and naval battles against named foreign coalitions.
They show enemy groups travelling with families and ox-carts.
The accompanying text names states destroyed before the attack on Egypt.
The naval scene is the earliest detailed depiction of a sea battle.
The groups' headdresses can be matched to specific ethnic origins.

milestones.text: The University of Chicago's Epigraphic Survey begins recording the temple's reliefs and inscriptions; the Sea Peoples scenes are published in 1930.

summary: Ramesses III's temple reliefs depicting land and sea battles against the Sea Peoples — the key source for the Bronze Age Collapse.
significance: The main contemporary record of the "Sea Peoples", and key evidence for the collapse of the Bronze Age world around 1200 BC.
body:
Carved sandstone reliefs and inscriptions on the mortuary temple of Pharaoh Ramesses III at Medinet Habu, on the west bank of the Nile at Thebes (Luxor), made around 1175 BC. They are still in place, and were recorded and published by the University of Chicago's Epigraphic Survey from 1924.

They celebrate Ramesses' victory over a coalition of invaders the Egyptians named Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh — the groups modern scholars call the "Sea Peoples". The naval scene, the earliest detailed picture of a sea battle, shows Egyptian archers trapping enemy ships against the shore, with men falling into the water. The land scene shows the enemy travelling with ox-carts carrying women and children, suggesting a migration of whole peoples rather than a raid. Different groups are shown with distinct feathered or horned headgear.

The inscription claims that before reaching Egypt these peoples destroyed Hatti (the Hittite Empire), Kode, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya (Cyprus). That list matches the destruction layers archaeologists find across Anatolia and the Levant around 1200 BC.

It is royal propaganda, and its numbers and claims of total victory need caution. The Peleset are usually identified with the Philistines, who settled on the coast of Canaan soon after.

name: The last letters of Ugarit

claims.text: Ugaritic letters record enemy ships attacking while defensive forces were absent.
Some tablets were found in a kiln, apparently never dispatched.
Ugaritic scribes used an early alphabetic cuneiform script.
Ugarit's royal archives also preserve extensive mythological and religious texts, including the Baal Cycle, alongside the administrative and diplomatic correspondence.

milestones.text: A farmer ploughing near Ras Shamra breaks into a tomb, leading to the discovery of Ugarit.
Claude Schaeffer begins decades of excavation, recovering the city's archives.

summary: Cuneiform tablets recording a city's final weeks — including letters found still in the kiln, never sent.
significance: A rare first-hand record of a city's final days during the Bronze Age collapse, from one of the richest archives of the ancient Near East.
body:
Clay tablets inscribed in cuneiform from the archives of Ugarit, a wealthy trading city on the Syrian coast, written around 1190–1185 BC, just before the city was destroyed. Ugarit was found in 1928 and excavated from 1929 by Claude Schaeffer; the tablets are now divided between museums in Damascus, Aleppo and the Louvre.

The last letters show a kingdom under attack. King Ammurapi writes to the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) that enemy ships have arrived and burned his towns while his own troops are away in the Hittite lands and his ships are off the coast of Lycia. Another letter warns that seven enemy ships have done great damage. The enemies are not named, but they are often linked to the "Sea Peoples" recorded in Egypt.

Some of these tablets were long said to have been found still in a kiln, baked for dispatch when the city fell; later study has questioned this, but the letters clearly date from the city's final crisis.

Ugarit's archives matter far beyond its end. Its scribes developed an alphabet of about thirty cuneiform signs, one of the earliest alphabets anywhere. And its religious texts, including the Baal Cycle about the storm god, are the main source for Canaanite myth before the Hebrew Bible.

name: The Dipylon Amphora

claims.text: The Dipylon Amphora served as a grave marker in the Athenian Kerameikos.
It depicts a prothesis, the laying out of the dead.
It marks the reappearance of figural scenes in Greek art in the 8th century BC.
It marked the grave of a woman.
The amphora belongs to a workshop tradition, the Dipylon Master and his circle, credited with several of the finest and largest surviving Geometric grave vases.

milestones.text: Dug up in Ioannis Palaiologos' excavations in the outer Kerameikos, Athens, and bought for the national collection.

summary: A 1.55 m Geometric grave marker showing a funeral scene — the return of the human figure to Greek art.
significance: A monument of Geometric Athens and the return of the human figure — and of storytelling — to Greek art after the Dark Age.
body:
A painted pottery amphora 1.55 m tall, made in Athens around 760–750 BC as a grave marker for a woman. It came from the Dipylon cemetery in the Kerameikos, Athens, dug up in Ioannis Palaiologos' excavations of 1871–72, and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens. A hole in its base let offerings of liquid reach the grave below.

Most of its surface is covered in bands of meander (key-pattern) and zigzags, the hallmark of the Geometric style. In the panel between the handles is a *prothesis*, the laying out of the dead: the body lies on a bier under a raised shroud, and mourners stand on either side with both hands raised to their heads in the gesture of grief.

The figures are reduced to triangles and lines, but they are people doing something specific. After four centuries in which Greek pottery carried only abstract patterns, this marks the return of human figures and scenes to Greek art. Within a few generations, painters would be telling stories from myth and from Homer.

It is the masterpiece of a painter known as the Dipylon Master, whose workshop made the largest and finest Geometric grave vases. Such vessels stood on the tombs of Athens' wealthiest families as permanent public monuments.

name: The Dipylon Oinochoe

claims.text: The Dipylon Oinochoe bears one of the earliest known Greek alphabetic inscriptions.
The inscription offers the vessel as a prize for dancing.
The text appears to be metrical.
The earliest Greek inscriptions are non-administrative in content.

milestones.text: Found in the Dipylon cemetery of the Kerameikos, Athens; its scratched verse is among the oldest alphabetic Greek inscriptions.

summary: A wine jug carrying one of the earliest Greek alphabetic inscriptions — a prize for the best dancer.
significance: One of the earliest examples of the Greek alphabet — used not for accounts, but for a line of verse about a dancing prize.
body:
A plain wine jug (oinochoe) of painted pottery, made in Athens around 740 BC. It was found in 1871 in a grave in the Dipylon cemetery of the Kerameikos, Athens, and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Around its shoulder, early Attic letters running from right to left were scratched after firing: "whoever of all the dancers now dances most gracefully…". The rest is hard to read, but seems to offer the jug as the prize. The words form a line of hexameter, the metre of epic poetry.

The inscription dates to within a generation or so of the Greeks' adoption of the alphabet from the Phoenicians, probably in the early 8th century BC. It is a striking contrast with Linear B, the Mycenaean script of five centuries earlier, which was used only for palace bookkeeping. From the start, Greeks used their new alphabet to record verse, names and play — the things they valued in ordinary social life.

The jug itself is unremarkable; its importance lies entirely in the few words scratched on it. With Nestor's Cup from Pithekoussai, it is among the oldest surviving Greek verse inscriptions.

name: Nestor's Cup

claims.text: The cup bears a three-line inscription largely in hexameter verse.
The inscription alludes to a cup described in the Iliad.
It was found in a child's burial at Pithekoussai and dates to c. 730–720 BC.
It demonstrates knowledge of Homeric material in the western Mediterranean by that date.

milestones.text: Found by Giorgio Buchner in a child's cremation grave in the San Montano cemetery of Pithekoussai.

summary: A drinking cup from a Greek colony in Italy inscribed with a joke that assumes the audience knows Homer.
significance: One of the earliest Greek inscriptions and the earliest witness to the Homeric epics — a joke that assumed its readers knew the Iliad.
body:
A small pottery drinking cup made in Rhodes and inscribed around 730–720 BC. Giorgio Buchner found it in 1954 in a child's cremation grave at Pithekoussai, one of the earliest Greek trading settlements in the west, on the island of Ischia off the Bay of Naples. It is now in the island's archaeological museum.

Scratched on its side, in three lines in the Euboean form of the alphabet, mostly in hexameter verse, is a joke: "I am the cup of Nestor, good to drink from. Whoever drinks from this cup, desire for beautiful-crowned Aphrodite will seize him at once." In the *Iliad*, Nestor owns a massive gold cup so heavy that only he can lift it full; this cup is small, cheap clay, mock-heroically claiming the same name.

The joke only works if drinkers knew the Homeric story. So around 725 BC, Greek settlers far from the Aegean were literate enough to write playful verse, and familiar enough with epic poetry to enjoy a parody of it. Whether the reference is to the *Iliad* itself or to the wider tradition behind it is debated.

Why a cup carrying an adult drinking-party joke was buried with a child is unknown.

name: The Lefkandi Centaur

claims.text: The Lefkandi Centaur dates to c. 900 BC and is the earliest known Greek centaur image.
Its head and body were found in two separate graves.
A notch was deliberately cut into one knee.
The figure represents Cheiron.

milestones.text: Found by the British School at Athens in the Toumba cemetery: the head in one grave and the body in another, three metres away.

summary: A terracotta centaur of c. 900 BC — the earliest known image of a mythological hybrid in Greek art, deliberately broken and buried in two graves.
significance: The earliest known image of a Greek mythological creature, made two centuries before any surviving text mentions centaurs.
body:
A painted terracotta figure of a centaur, 36 cm tall, made in the late 10th century BC, during the so-called Dark Age. It was found in 1969 by the British School at Athens in the Toumba cemetery at Lefkandi on Euboea, and is now in the Archaeological Museum of Eretria.

The figure has a human chest, arms and head joined to a horse's body, and is painted with geometric patterns. It is hollow and was made on a potter's wheel. One knee carries a deliberate cut. Its head was found in one grave and its body in another nearby: someone had broken it on purpose and divided it between two burials, presumably for reasons connected with the people buried there.

The knee wound has suggested Cheiron, the wise centaur who taught Achilles and was accidentally wounded by Heracles. If so, this would be the earliest image of a named Greek myth, but the identification cannot be proved.

Either way, the figure shows that the mythical world later described by Homer and Hesiod was already part of Greek imagination around 900 BC. Its quality also adds to the evidence from Lefkandi that the Dark Age was not as poor or isolated as once thought.

name: Lydian electrum stater

claims.text: The earliest standardised stamped coins were produced in Lydia in the late 7th century BC.
They were struck in naturally occurring electrum.
Croesus introduced separate refined gold and silver coinages.
The variable composition of electrum limited its reliability as money.

milestones.text: David Hogarth's excavation of the temple of Artemis at Ephesus finds a foundation deposit of electrum coins, the earliest well-dated coinage.

summary: The earliest standardised coinage: lumps of natural gold-silver alloy stamped with a lion's head.
significance: The first true coins: a Lydian invention that the Greek cities took up within decades and made a symbol of civic identity.
body:
Coins of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, struck in the kingdom of Lydia in western Asia Minor between about 630 and 560 BC. Some of the earliest well-dated examples were found in 1904–05 in a foundation deposit of the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. Examples are held in the British Museum and many other collections.

Electrum washed down the Pactolus river at the Lydian capital, Sardis — the river in which King Midas, in myth, washed off his golden touch. The innovation was to cut it into pieces of fixed weight and stamp them with a mark of authority, so they could be counted instead of weighed and tested at every exchange. The earliest marks were simple striations; the best-known coins carry a lion's head, emblem of the Lydian royal house.

Because natural electrum varies in its gold content, the coins' true value was uncertain. Under King Croesus (c. 560–546 BC), Lydia began striking separate coins of refined gold and silver, the first two-metal currency.

The Greek cities of Ionia, such as Miletus and Ephesus, copied the idea almost at once, with their own civic badges. Within a century coinage had spread across the Greek world, and coins became a mark of each city's identity.

name: The Chigi Vase
museum: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome

claims.text: The Chigi Vase depicts hoplites in formation with aspis shields and thrusting spears.
It includes a piper accompanying the advance.
It dates to c. 650–640 BC and is Protocorinthian work.
It depicts a fully developed phalanx as later understood.

milestones.text: Found in fragments in an Etruscan tomb at Monte Aguzzo, on Prince Mario Chigi's estate.

summary: A Corinthian olpe carrying the earliest detailed depiction of hoplites fighting in formation.
significance: The earliest detailed picture of hoplites fighting in formation, and a masterpiece of Corinthian miniature painting.
body:
A painted pottery jug (olpe) 26 cm tall, made in Corinth around 650–640 BC. It was found in 1881 in an Etruscan tomb at Monte Aguzzo near Veii, north of Rome, on the estate of Prince Mario Chigi, and is now in the National Etruscan Museum at the Villa Giulia, Rome.

It is painted in the Protocorinthian miniature style, with figures only a few centimetres high, in several colours rather than plain silhouette. Its most famous band shows two lines of heavily armed infantrymen — hoplites — advancing on each other with round shields, crested helmets, greaves and spears held overhand, while a piper plays to keep them in step. A second group is still running up to join the line. Other bands show a lion hunt, a hare hunt, horsemen and a scene often read as the Judgement of Paris.

The vase is the key image in the debate over the hoplite phalanx: whether this close-packed way of fighting appeared suddenly in the 7th century BC as a "hoplite reform", or developed gradually. It shows that something like a formation of armoured infantry existed by the mid-7th century.

Its findspot in an Etruscan tomb shows how Greek luxury goods were reaching Italy through trade.

name: The François Vase

claims.text: The François Vase is signed by the painter Kleitias and the potter Ergotimos.
It carries over 270 figures with more than 120 identifying inscriptions.
It was found in an Etruscan tomb, showing Athenian pottery export to Italy.
It preserves versions of myths that differ from later canonical accounts.

milestones.text: Found in fragments by Alessandro François in an Etruscan tomb near Chiusi.
A museum attendant smashes it into 638 pieces; it is reassembled, and restored again in 1973.

summary: An Attic black-figure krater carrying over 270 figures in six friezes, signed by both its potter and its painter.
significance: A picture-book of Greek myth as it stood around 570 BC, and the masterpiece of early Athenian black-figure painting.
body:
A large black-figure krater (wine-mixing bowl), 66 cm tall, made in Athens around 570–565 BC and signed twice each by the potter Ergotimos and the painter Kleitias. It was exported to Etruria, found by Alessandro François in 1844 in a tomb near Chiusi, and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Florence.

Six bands of decoration carry more than 270 human and animal figures, over 120 of them labelled with their names. The central scene is the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, attended by the gods; around it run the Calydonian boar hunt, the funeral games for Patroclus, Achilles pursuing the Trojan prince Troilus, Theseus and the young Athenians dancing after their escape from the Minotaur, and the battle of the Lapiths and centaurs. The vase is thus an illustrated encyclopaedia of myth, preserving versions of stories before later poets fixed them differently.

It was made for drinking parties, not display: a bowl for mixing wine with water at a banquet. Its export to an Etruscan family shows the prestige of Athenian painted pottery in Italy.

In 1900 a museum guard smashed it into 638 pieces with a stool. It was reassembled, and restored again in 1973 using better methods.

name: The Euphronios Krater

claims.text: The krater is signed by the painter Euphronios and potter Euxitheos.
It depicts the recovery of Sarpedon's body as described in the Iliad.
It was illegally excavated from an Etruscan tomb and later repatriated to Italy.
The case materially changed museum acquisition practice.

milestones.text: Looted from an Etruscan tomb near Cerveteri.
Bought by the Metropolitan Museum of Art for a then-record $1 million, with a false provenance.
Returned to Italy after an investigation into its looting.

summary: A red-figure krater showing the death of Sarpedon — a masterpiece of Greek vase painting, and the object that changed museum acquisition ethics.
significance: A masterpiece of early red-figure painting — and the looted object whose return changed how museums acquire antiquities.
body:
A red-figure calyx krater (wine-mixing bowl), made in Athens around 515 BC and signed by the painter Euphronios and the potter Euxitheos. It is now in the National Etruscan Museum at Cerveteri, Italy.

Its main scene comes from *Iliad* Book 16: the winged figures of Sleep and Death lift the body of the Trojan ally Sarpedon, son of Zeus, from the battlefield, while Hermes watches. Blood runs from Sarpedon's wounds. Euphronios belonged to the "Pioneer Group" of Athenian painters who explored the new red-figure technique, in which figures were left in the red of the clay and details drawn with a brush. That freedom let him show muscles, twisting poses and foreshortening in a way the older black-figure silhouettes could not.

The krater was looted from an Etruscan tomb near Cerveteri in 1971. In 1972 the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York bought it for $1 million, then a record for any ancient work, with a false story that it came from an old family collection. After an Italian investigation into the antiquities trade, the Met returned it to Italy in 2008.

The case, with others, led museums to adopt much stricter rules on the provenance of the antiquities they buy.

name: The Kroisos Kouros

claims.text: The Kroisos Kouros is a marble grave statue of c. 530 BC from Attica.
Its base bears an inscription naming Kroisos as killed in battle.
The kouros form derives from Egyptian sculptural conventions.
Archaic Greek marble sculpture was painted.

milestones.text: Illegally dug up from a grave mound at Anavyssos, cut into pieces and smuggled to Paris.
Traced to a Paris dealer by Greek authorities, returned and reassembled in Athens with its inscribed base.

summary: A grave statue of a young man killed in battle, with an inscription asking the passer-by to mourn him.
significance: One of the finest Archaic kouroi, and a rare one that names the person it commemorates: a young man killed in battle.
body:
A marble statue of a nude young man (a kouros), 1.95 m tall, made around 530–520 BC as a grave marker in Attica. It was dug up illegally at Anavyssos, south of Athens, in 1936 and smuggled to Paris in pieces; Greek authorities recovered it in 1937. It is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens, with its inscribed base.

The figure stands with the left foot forward and arms at his sides, wearing the faint "Archaic smile". The pose comes from Egyptian statues, which Greeks saw at trading posts such as Naukratis, but the Greek figure stands free without a supporting back pillar and is carved fully in the round. Compared with earlier kouroi, its body is softer and more naturally modelled. Traces of paint show that hair, eyes and lips were coloured.

The base carries a verse epitaph: "Stand and mourn at the monument of dead Kroisos, whom raging Ares destroyed one day as he fought in the front ranks." So the statue is not a god or a general type but a memorial to one particular young man, probably from a wealthy Athenian family.

Kouroi served both as grave markers and as offerings in sanctuaries; within a few decades the type gave way to the more relaxed poses of Classical sculpture.

name: The Peplos Kore

claims.text: The Peplos Kore was buried in the Acropolis debris after the Persian sack of 480 BC.
Substantial original pigment survives on the statue.
Her garment is an ependytes associated with divine imagery rather than a peplos.
The statue represents a goddess rather than a mortal woman.

milestones.text: Found on the Acropolis in the debris the Athenians buried after the Persian sack of 480 BC.

summary: A painted marble statue of a young woman from the Acropolis, buried after the Persian sack — and probably a goddess, not a girl.
significance: The best-preserved painted Archaic statue, and the clearest proof that Greek sculpture was brightly coloured, not white.
body:
A marble statue of a young woman (a kore), 1.2 m tall, made in Athens around 530 BC and dedicated on the Acropolis. It was found in 1886 in the "Persian debris" — the broken statues and buildings the Athenians buried after the Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC. It is now in the Acropolis Museum, Athens.

Korai were standing female statues that wealthy Athenians dedicated to the gods, and dozens were found in the same debris. This one is named for her garment, once thought to be a peplos, a simple woollen dress. It is now usually identified as an *ependytes*, a decorated overgarment worn by images of goddesses. Her missing left forearm, made separately, held out an object, so she may be a goddess, probably Athena or Artemis, rather than a girl.

Because she was buried soon after being damaged, much of her paint survived: patterned bands on her dress, coloured hair, eyes and lips, and holes for metal attachments. Reconstructions using ultraviolet light and pigment analysis show a strikingly colourful figure.

She is a key piece of evidence that Greek marble sculpture was painted, contrary to the white-marble image of antiquity created in later centuries.

name: The Parthenon Frieze

claims.text: The Parthenon frieze is a continuous relief over 160 m long with hundreds of figures.
The relief depth was varied to compensate for the viewing angle from below.
Approximately half the surviving frieze is in the British Museum.
The frieze depicts the Panathenaic procession.
Elgin's permit authorised removal of the sculptures.

milestones.text: Agents of Lord Elgin remove about half the surviving frieze under an Ottoman permit.
Bought by Parliament from Elgin for £35,000 and placed in the British Museum.
The new Acropolis Museum opens, displaying the frieze blocks held in Athens with space left for those in London.

summary: A 160 m continuous relief of a procession — and the most contested cultural property dispute in the world.
significance: The masterpiece of Classical relief sculpture — and the most famous dispute in the world over the return of cultural property.
body:
A carved marble frieze that ran for 160 m around the top of the inner walls of the Parthenon in Athens, made around 442–438 BC under the direction of Pheidias as part of Pericles' building programme. About half of what survives is in the British Museum, London; most of the rest is in the Acropolis Museum, Athens.

It shows a single great procession, with about 380 human figures and more than 200 animals: horsemen in ranks, chariots, elders, musicians, girls carrying vessels and cattle led to sacrifice. Over the east entrance, seated gods watch as a folded cloth is handled. The scene is usually identified as the Panathenaic procession bringing a new robe to Athena — unusual, since Greek temple sculpture normally showed myth, not citizens. The relief is only a few centimetres deep, carved slightly deeper at the top to be legible from far below.

The building later became a church and a mosque, and was badly damaged in an explosion in 1687. Between 1801 and 1812 agents of Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, removed about half the surviving frieze; the British Museum bought it in 1816. Whether his Ottoman permit allowed this is disputed.

Greece has long sought the frieze's return. The Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, displays the Athens blocks with space left for those in London.

name: The Discobolus

claims.text: The Discobolus is known only from Roman copies of a lost Greek bronze by Myron.
Almost all large Greek bronzes were lost to melting down.
Marble copies require structural supports absent in the bronze original.
The depicted throwing action is biomechanically accurate.

milestones.text: The Lancellotti Discobolus, the best Roman copy, is found on a Lancellotti family estate.
Sold to Nazi Germany and displayed in Munich; returned to Italy in 1948.

summary: Myron's discus thrower, caught at the instant of maximum coiled tension — known only through Roman copies.
significance: The most famous athletic statue of antiquity: a solution to the problem of showing violent movement in still sculpture.
body:
A statue of an athlete throwing the discus, made in bronze by the sculptor Myron around 460–450 BC. The original is lost; it is known from Roman marble copies, the best being the Lancellotti Discobolus, found on the Esquiline in Rome in 1781 and now in the Palazzo Massimo, Rome. Another is in the British Museum.

The athlete is caught at the top of his backswing, the moment of stillness just before he unwinds to throw. His body forms two crossing arcs, so the figure holds both tension and balance. His face is calm, in keeping with the Classical ideal that a hero should show composure rather than strain. Sports scientists debate whether the pose is a realistic throwing position.

Like almost all large Greek bronzes, Myron's original was later melted down for its metal. The marble copies need a tree trunk and other supports that the stronger bronze did not.

The statue's later history reflects its fame. In 1938 Mussolini's government sold the Lancellotti copy to Hitler, who displayed it in Munich as an image of the ideal body; it was returned to Italy in 1948.

name: The Doryphoros

claims.text: The Doryphoros was made by Polykleitos to demonstrate his written Canon of proportion.
It uses contrapposto with alternating tension and relaxation across the body.
The bronze original is lost and it survives through Roman marble copies.
The Canon's exact proportional ratios can be reconstructed.

milestones.text: The best-preserved Roman copy is found at Pompeii, traditionally in the Samnite Palaestra.

summary: Polykleitos' "Spear Bearer" — a statue made to demonstrate a written theory of ideal proportion.
significance: The model of the ideal human body in Classical art, made to demonstrate a written theory of proportion and copied for two thousand years.
body:
A bronze statue of a young man carrying a spear, made by the sculptor Polykleitos of Argos around 440 BC. The original is lost. It is known from Roman marble copies, the best preserved found at Pompeii in 1797 and now in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

Polykleitos wrote a treatise, the *Canon*, setting out the mathematical proportions of the perfect human body, and made this statue to put it into practice. The treatise is lost too, but the pairing of written theory and demonstration piece is unique in ancient art.

The statue's key feature is contrapposto. The weight rests on the right leg, so the right hip rises and the right shoulder drops; the left leg is relaxed and the left arm once held the spear. Tension and relaxation balance each other diagonally across the body. This is what makes Classical figures look alive and poised where Archaic kouroi look rigid and frontal.

The Pompeii copy stood in an exercise ground, where young men trained in sight of the ideal they aimed for. Roman sculptors copied the type constantly, Renaissance artists studied it, and its proportions were still taught in art academies in the 19th century.

name: The Riace Bronzes
museum: Museo Nazionale della Magna Grecia, Reggio Calabria

claims.text: The Riace Bronzes are original Greek bronze statues of the mid-5th century BC.
They incorporate copper, silver and ivory inlays for lips, teeth and eyes.
They were recovered from the sea off Calabria in 1972.
They were part of a cargo of Greek art being shipped to Italy.
The figures can be identified with specific known statues or heroes.

milestones.text: Spotted on the seabed by a snorkelling tourist, Stefano Mariottini, and raised days later.
First shown to the public after conservation in Florence, drawing huge crowds.

summary: Two life-size Greek bronze warriors recovered from the sea in 1972 — original Classical bronzes, not copies.
significance: Two of the very few large Greek bronzes to survive as originals, showing what Classical sculpture really looked like before Roman marble copies.
body:
Two life-size bronze statues of nude warriors, about 2 m tall, made in Greece around 460–450 BC. They were spotted on the seabed off Riace in Calabria, southern Italy, by a snorkeller in 1972, probably lost overboard from an ancient ship. After conservation in Florence they were first shown in 1981, and are now in the National Museum of Magna Graecia, Reggio Calabria.

Both men stand with their weight on one leg, once holding shields and spears. Statue A is younger and more intense, with lips slightly parted; Statue B is older and calmer. Who they represent, and whether they come from a single monument, is debated.

Almost everything known about Classical sculpture comes from Roman marble copies; the Greek bronze originals were nearly all melted down for metal. These are originals, and the difference is striking. Freshly cast, the bronze was golden-brown, not green. Lips and nipples are inlaid in copper, teeth in silver, and the eyes in ivory and coloured stone, giving a lifelike effect no marble copy reproduces. Clay from the original casting was still sealed inside them.

They are among the most important finds of Greek art made in the 20th century.

name: The Charioteer of Delphi

claims.text: The Charioteer was dedicated c. 474 BC to commemorate a chariot race victory.
It survived because it was buried by a landslide at Delphi.
The eyes are inlaid with onyx and glass paste, with copper eyelashes.
It formed part of a larger group including a chariot and horses.

milestones.text: Found by the French School at Athens during the 'Great Excavation' of the sanctuary at Delphi.

summary: A surviving bronze from a victory monument, buried by a landslide and preserved with its inlaid eyes intact.
significance: One of the finest surviving Greek bronzes, and the classic example of the restrained Severe Style between Archaic and Classical art.
body:
A life-size bronze statue of a chariot driver, 1.8 m tall, from a victory monument dedicated at Delphi around 474 BC. It was found in 1896 by the French School at Athens during the great excavation of the sanctuary, and is now in the Delphi Archaeological Museum.

The inscription on its base records a dedication by Polyzalus, a tyrant of Gela in Sicily, to celebrate a chariot victory in the Pythian Games. The driver was part of a group with a four-horse chariot and perhaps a groom, of which only fragments survive. He stands upright in a long belted robe, holding the reins, probably shown on the lap of honour after the race.

The figure survived because it was buried by a rockfall, perhaps in the earthquake of 373 BC, while nearly all other Greek bronzes were melted down. Its eyes, inlaid with stone and glass and fringed with copper lashes, are intact, as are copper lips and a silver-inlaid headband.

The statue belongs to the Severe Style of about 480–450 BC, between the stiffness of Archaic sculpture and the ease of the Classical. The deep vertical folds of the robe make him look like a fluted column, and his calm face shows victory without display.

name: Ostraka

claims.text: Athenians voted for ostracism by scratching names on pottery sherds.
Over 11,000 ostraka have been excavated in Athens.
A cache of 190 sherds naming Themistocles was written in only fourteen hands.
Ostracism exiled a man for ten years without loss of property or citizenship.

milestones.text: American School excavations of the Athenian Agora begin, eventually recovering over a thousand ostraka.
German excavators in the Kerameikos find a deposit of about 9,000 ostraka dumped in an old channel of the Eridanos.

summary: Broken pottery used as ballots in ostracism votes — democracy's discarded paperwork, recovered by the thousand.
significance: The ballots of Athenian democracy, surviving by the thousand — direct evidence of how ordinary citizens voted, and of early vote-rigging.
body:
Broken pieces of pottery used as ballots in ostracism votes in Athens between 487 and about 415 BC. More than 11,000 have been found, chiefly in the American School's excavations of the Agora from 1931 and in a deposit of about 9,000 found in the Kerameikos in 1966–69. They are in the Agora and Kerameikos museums, Athens.

Ostracism was introduced in the reforms of Cleisthenes. Once a year the Assembly decided whether to hold one. If it did, each citizen scratched on a potsherd the name of a man he wanted removed. If at least 6,000 votes were cast, the man named most often was exiled for ten years. He kept his property and citizenship and could return afterwards without disgrace. It was a way of removing a dangerously powerful or divisive politician without a trial.

The sherds carry the names of the leading men of the age — Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Megacles, Pericles' rivals — sometimes with insults or crude drawings added. A cache of 190 ostraka naming Themistocles, found in a well on the Acropolis slope, was written by only fourteen hands: someone was preparing ballots in bulk for others to cast.

The last ostracism, of Hyperbolus around 415 BC, ended the practice.

name: Athenian owl tetradrachm

claims.text: Athenian tetradrachms were struck from Laurion silver with consistent weight and purity.
They circulated widely across the Mediterranean and Near East.
The design was kept deliberately archaic for recognisability.
Athens required subject allies to use Athenian coinage and measures.
Emergency plated coinage was issued late in the Peloponnesian War.

summary: Athena on one side, her owl on the other — the ancient Mediterranean's first international reserve currency.
significance: The most trusted coin of the Classical world, and an instrument of Athenian power: the first currency used far beyond its own state.
body:
A silver coin worth four drachmas, about 17 grams, issued by Athens from around 510 BC until the 1st century BC. Examples survive in collections worldwide and turn up in hoards from Egypt to Afghanistan.

The front shows the head of Athena in a crested helmet; the back shows her owl, an olive sprig and the letters ΑΘΕ, for "of the Athenians". The coins were struck from silver mined at Laurion in southern Attica, and their reliable weight and purity made them accepted across the Mediterranean and Near East, where they were often imitated. The design was deliberately left old-fashioned for centuries after Greek art had moved on: a familiar coin was a trusted one.

The coins also served Athenian power. In the 5th century BC Athens ordered the members of its Delian League empire to use Athenian coins, weights and measures, suppressing local mints. The tribute paid by allies, minted into owls, helped fund the fleet and the buildings of the Acropolis.

When silver ran short at the end of the Peloponnesian War, Athens issued bronze coins plated with silver. Aristophanes' *Frogs* (405 BC) jokes that the city prefers bad coins to good — an early statement of what is now called Gresham's law.

name: The Tomb of the Diver

claims.text: The Tomb of the Diver contains the only known Greek painted figural tomb scenes of c. 480 BC.
The wall panels depict a symposium.
Greek monumental painting is otherwise almost entirely lost.
The diving figure symbolises the passage from life to death.

milestones.text: Found by Mario Napoli in a small cemetery near Paestum.

summary: Five painted slabs from a tomb at Paestum — the only surviving Greek painted tomb with figural scenes from this era.
significance: One of the very few surviving examples of Greek painting from the Classical period, an art otherwise known only from texts and vases.
body:
A stone burial chest (cist tomb) with five painted limestone slabs, made around 480–470 BC at Poseidonia (Paestum), a Greek colony in southern Italy. It was found in 1968 by Mario Napoli in a small cemetery near the city, and is now in the National Archaeological Museum of Paestum.

The four side walls show a symposium, the Greek drinking party: men recline on couches, drinking, talking, playing the lyre and the game of *kottabos*, flicking wine dregs at a target, while a young man plays the double pipe and others arrive. On the underside of the lid, facing the dead man, a lone young man dives from a stone platform into water, between two trees.

Greek painters such as Polygnotus were famous in antiquity, but their works are lost, and Greek painting is known mainly from descriptions and from vase painting. This tomb is one of the only surviving examples of Greek painting on a wall from the period.

The diver is usually read as an image of passing from life into death, perhaps linked to the mystery religions and Pythagorean ideas popular in southern Italy. Nothing in the tomb confirms this, and the meaning of the single scene remains open.

name: The Sarissa

claims.text: The sarissa was a two-handed pike substantially longer than a hoplite spear.
Iron sarissa fittings including joining sleeves have been excavated in Macedon.
Its use required a smaller shield strapped to the arm.
Pikes of the first several ranks projected beyond the front of the formation.
The sarissa reached lengths of six metres or more.

summary: A pike up to six metres long, wielded two-handed — the weapon that made Macedon the dominant military power.
significance: The weapon that made the Macedonian phalanx unbeatable for over a century, from Philip II's conquests to the Roman victory at Pydna.
body:
The long pike of the Macedonian infantry, introduced by Philip II after 359 BC and used until the Roman conquest of Macedon in 168 BC. Iron heads, butt-spikes and joining sleeves have been excavated at Vergina and other Macedonian sites.

The sarissa was made of cornel wood, about 5–6 m long — roughly twice the length of a hoplite spear — probably in two sections joined by an iron sleeve. It had an iron head and a heavy bronze butt-spike that balanced it and could be stuck in the ground. It weighed around 6 kg and needed both hands, so the soldier carried only a small shield strapped to his forearm and shoulder.

That trade-off defined the Macedonian phalanx. A single pikeman was nearly defenceless, but a formation was almost impossible to attack from the front, because the pikes of the first five ranks projected beyond the front line. Using it needed constant drill, which is why Philip turned the Macedonian army from a seasonal levy into a professional force.

The phalanx needed flat ground and an unbroken line. Combined with cavalry under Philip and Alexander it conquered from Greece to India, but when it lost its supports the more flexible Roman legions defeated it at Cynoscephalae (197 BC) and Pydna (168 BC).

name: The Vergina Larnax
museum: Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai, Vergina

claims.text: The gold larnax was found in the unlooted Tomb II at Vergina in 1977.
It contained cremated bones, purple-dyed cloth and a gold oak wreath.
The lid bears the sixteen-rayed Argead star emblem.
The remains are those of Philip II.
A second, smaller gold larnax was found in an adjoining chamber of the same tomb, believed to hold the remains of a queen or princess.

milestones.text: Found by Manolis Andronikos in a marble sarcophagus in the unlooted Tomb II at Vergina.

summary: A solid gold burial casket embossed with the Macedonian star, holding cremated royal bones and a gold oak wreath.
significance: The centrepiece of the richest unlooted royal tomb in Greece, and possibly the casket of Philip II, father of Alexander the Great.
body:
A solid gold casket (larnax) weighing about 11 kg, made in Macedon around 336–316 BC. Manolis Andronikos found it in 1977 inside a marble sarcophagus in the main chamber of Tomb II, beneath the Great Tumulus at Vergina, ancient Aigai, the old royal capital of Macedon. It is now in the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai at Vergina.

The lid is embossed with a sixteen-rayed star, the emblem of the Macedonian royal house. Inside were cremated bones wrapped in a cloth of purple and gold, with a gold wreath of oak leaves and acorns. A second, smaller gold larnax in the antechamber held the bones of a young woman, wrapped in a similar cloth with a gold diadem.

Whose bones they are is debated. Philip II, assassinated in 336 BC, is the leading candidate, supported by the tomb's date, its wealth, and small ivory portrait heads found nearby. Others argue for Alexander's half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus, buried in 316 BC. Studies of the skeletons have reached opposite conclusions.

The star on the lid has become a powerful national symbol in Greece and in the dispute over the name "Macedonia".

name: The Vergina hunt frieze
museum: Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai, Vergina

claims.text: The Tomb II façade carries a painted hunting frieze 5.6 m wide.
It employs perspective, foreshortening and shading.
Greek monumental painting of this period is otherwise almost entirely lost.
Lion hunting carried Persian royal associations.
The frieze depicts Philip II and Alexander.

milestones.text: Manolis Andronikos uncovers the painted façade of Tomb II beneath the Great Tumulus at Vergina.
