summary: A painted hunting scene above the door of Tomb II — a rare survival of Greek monumental painting at its height.
significance: The finest surviving example of ancient Greek painting at its peak, a level otherwise known only from descriptions by ancient writers.
body:
A painted frieze 5.6 m wide across the façade of Tomb II at Vergina (ancient Aigai) in Macedon, made around 336–316 BC. Manolis Andronikos uncovered it in 1977 beneath the Great Tumulus; it remains on the tomb, within the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai.

Ten hunters on foot and horseback, with dogs, pursue a lion, a boar and deer through a landscape of rocks and bare trees. The painter uses depth, foreshortened bodies, shading and cast shadows — the techniques ancient writers praised in famous painters such as Apelles and Zeuxis, whose works are entirely lost. Analysis has shown a broad range of pigments, including Egyptian blue. Almost nothing else survives to show what Greek painting at this level looked like.

The subject carries a political message. Lion hunting was a pursuit of Persian and Near Eastern kings, so showing Macedonian royals hunting lions claimed a grand, eastern-style kingship. A bearded central rider and a youth on horseback have been identified as Philip II and the young Alexander, which is plausible but cannot be proved.

The tomb also held the gold larnax with the cremated bones that may be Philip's.

name: The Alexander Mosaic

claims.text: The Alexander Mosaic is composed of over a million tesserae.
It was found in the House of the Faun at Pompeii.
It copies a lost Hellenistic Greek painting.
It uses a restricted four-colour palette described in ancient sources.
It depicts the battle of Issus rather than Gaugamela.

milestones.text: Found in the floor of an exedra in the House of the Faun.
Lifted and moved to the museum in Naples.

summary: A floor mosaic from Pompeii made of over a million tesserae, copying a lost Greek painting of Alexander facing Darius.
significance: The most famous image of Alexander the Great, and the closest surviving view of a lost masterpiece of Greek painting.
body:
A floor mosaic about 5.8 by 3.1 m, made of more than a million tiny stone pieces, laid around 120–100 BC in the House of the Faun, one of the grandest houses in Pompeii. It was uncovered in 1831, lifted and moved to Naples in 1843, and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

It shows Alexander's battle against the Persian king Darius III, probably at Issus in 333 BC. Alexander charges in from the left, bareheaded, spearing a Persian noble who has put himself between Alexander and the king. Darius, at the centre in his chariot, turns back with an arm outstretched as his driver whips the horses away. He is shown not as a coward but as a man watching a disaster he can no longer stop. A horse seen from behind, in bold foreshortening, anchors the middle of the scene.

The mosaic is a copy of a Greek painting made within a generation of the battle, perhaps by Philoxenos of Eretria, whom ancient writers say painted Alexander's battle against Darius. It uses the four colours — red, yellow, black and white — that Pliny says the great Greek painters favoured.

Almost no large Greek paintings survive, so this Roman-era copy is the best guide to what they were like.

name: The Alexander Sarcophagus

claims.text: The sarcophagus was excavated at Sidon and is not Alexander's own burial.
It depicts Greeks and Persians in battle and hunting together.
Substantial original polychrome pigment survives on the marble.
It was made for Abdalonymos of Sidon.

milestones.text: Found by Osman Hamdi Bey in the royal necropolis of Sidon and taken to Istanbul.

summary: A marble sarcophagus carved with Alexander in battle and hunting — with much of its original paint still visible.
significance: A masterpiece of Greek sculpture made for a Phoenician king, with some of the best-preserved original paint of any ancient marble.
body:
A marble sarcophagus about 3 m long, carved by Greek sculptors around 320–310 BC. Osman Hamdi Bey found it in 1887 in the royal cemetery of Sidon, in modern Lebanon, and it is now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums. It is called the Alexander Sarcophagus because Alexander appears on it, not because he was buried in it.

It was probably made for Abdalonymos, a man Alexander made king of Sidon in 332 BC. One long side shows Greeks and Persians in battle, with Alexander on horseback wearing a lion-skin helmet, probably at Issus. The other shows Greeks and Persians hunting a lion together — an image of partnership fitting for a local ruler who owed his throne to Alexander.

The carving is entirely Greek in style, a sign of how quickly local elites in the conquered Near East adopted Greek art as a mark of status. Unusually, much of its original paint survives: purple and yellow clothing, red blood, painted eyes and details. It is some of the best evidence that Greek marble sculpture was fully coloured, and that the white classical look is the result of paint wearing away.

It was one of the founding objects of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

name: Alexander tetradrachm

claims.text: Alexander's coinage showed Herakles in a lion skin and enthroned Zeus.
It was struck at mints across the empire on a common standard.
Cities continued striking Alexander-type coins for around two centuries after his death.
Hellenistic rulers introduced portraits of living monarchs on coinage.

summary: A single coin design struck from Greece to India, continuing for centuries after Alexander's death.
significance: The first truly international coinage, struck from Greece to India and for centuries after Alexander's death.
body:
A silver coin worth four drachmas issued by Alexander the Great from about 336 BC and copied by cities and kings until around 50 BC. Examples survive worldwide in huge numbers.

The front shows the hero Herakles wearing a lion's skin; the back shows Zeus seated on a throne, holding an eagle and a sceptre, with the inscription "of Alexander". The Macedonian kings claimed descent from Herakles, and over time the Herakles head came to look more and more like Alexander himself.

Alexander struck the coins on the Athenian weight standard, at some two dozen mints from Macedon to Babylon, using the vast silver and gold captured from the Persian treasuries. The result was the first currency used across the whole of the former Persian Empire and the Greek world. Because merchants trusted it, cities kept striking "Alexanders" for two centuries after his death.

His successors went a step further. Ptolemy I put Alexander's own portrait on coins and soon replaced it with his own — the beginning of showing living rulers on money. The coins' wide spread and long life also make them one of archaeologists' most useful tools for dating Hellenistic sites.

name: The Porus Medallion

claims.text: The medallion depicts a horseman with a pike attacking an elephant carrying two riders.
The reverse shows a figure in Macedonian dress holding a thunderbolt, crowned by Nike.
It was struck within a few years of the Hydaspes campaign.
The horseman is Alexander and the elephant carries Porus.
It constitutes a claim to divine status by Alexander.

milestones.text: Several examples come to light in a hoard found in Iraq.

summary: A silver decadrachm showing a horseman attacking an elephant — probably the only contemporary image of Alexander in battle.
significance: Probably the only image of Alexander made in his own lifetime that shows him in battle — and possibly claiming the powers of a god.
body:
A large silver coin, a decadrachm (ten drachmas), struck around 325–323 BC, probably at Babylon. Only a handful are known; several came from a hoard found in Iraq in 1973. The British Museum holds an example.

One side shows a horseman with a long lance attacking a war elephant carrying two men, one of whom turns to throw a spear. The other shows a standing figure in Macedonian armour holding a thunderbolt, the weapon of Zeus, while a small winged Victory flies in to crown him.

The battle scene is usually read as Alexander fighting the Indian king Porus at the Hydaspes river in 326 BC. If so, the coin is a contemporary image of the battle, unlike the Alexander Mosaic or later sculptures. The thunderbolt figure is more striking: a Macedonian king holding Zeus' weapon, crowned by Victory. Whether Alexander approved it, and what it says about his claims to divinity in his lifetime, is debated.

Its size and rarity suggest it was not ordinary money but a special issue, perhaps given as a reward to veterans of the Indian campaign.

name: The Antikythera Mechanism

claims.text: The mechanism contains at least 30 bronze gears and displays astronomical cycles.
It predicts eclipses using a Saros-cycle dial.
A pin-and-slot device models the variable speed of the Moon.
Inscriptions on the device function as operating instructions.
No comparable geared device survives for over a millennium afterwards.
It was built in a Rhodian workshop connected to Hipparchus.

milestones.text: Raised by sponge divers from a 1st-century BC shipwreck off Antikythera, along with bronze and marble statues.
Valerios Stais spots a gear wheel in one of the corroded fragments.
Derek de Solla Price's Gears from the Greeks gives the first reconstruction of its gearing.
CT scanning reveals hidden gears and thousands of characters of inscription.

summary: A geared bronze astronomical calculator from a shipwreck — technology with no known equal for over a thousand years.
significance: The most complex machine to survive from the ancient world: proof that Hellenistic astronomy was built into working geared technology, more than a thousand years before anything comparable appears again.
body:
A hand-cranked bronze calculator of about 150–100 BC, roughly the size of a shoebox and driven by at least 30 interlocking gears. It survives as 82 corroded fragments, raised in 1900–01 from a Roman-era shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese, which also carried bronze and marble statues.

Turning the handle moved dials on the front and back. The front showed the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac, the Moon's phase and the date in the Egyptian calendar. The back carried a spiral dial predicting eclipses over the 223-month Saros cycle, and a dial counting the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games, including the Olympics. A pin-and-slot gear reproduced the Moon's changing speed across the sky. Thousands of tiny inscribed letters served as its user's guide.

Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity survives for over a thousand years. The device implies a tradition of precision instrument-making that has otherwise left no trace. Rhodes, home of the astronomer Hipparchus and later of Posidonius, is the most often suggested source, but this is unproven. Its workings were recovered gradually, through X-ray and gamma-ray imaging in the 20th century and CT scanning from 2005. It is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

name: The Winged Victory of Samothrace

claims.text: The Nike was found on Samothrace in 1863 and reassembled from many fragments.
She stands on a marble ship's prow that was set in a water basin.
A matching right hand was identified in 1950.
The open hand indicates a gesture of salute rather than holding an object.
The statue commemorates a specific naval victory.

milestones.text: Found in fragments by the French consul Charles Champoiseau and sent to the Louvre.
The right hand is found on Samothrace and matched to the statue.

summary: Nike alighting on a warship's prow, wind driving her drapery back — the most dynamic surviving Greek sculpture.
significance: The most dramatic surviving Greek sculpture of movement, and one of the most famous works in the Louvre.
body:
A marble statue of Nike, goddess of victory, 2.4 m tall, set on the prow of a marble warship, made around 200–190 BC. The French consul Charles Champoiseau found it in fragments in 1863 at the Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, in the northern Aegean. It is now in the Louvre, Paris.

Nike lands on the ship's prow, wings swept back, her robe pressed against her body by the wind and streaming out behind her. The sculptor renders thin, wet-looking cloth clinging to the legs and torso with extraordinary skill. The figure turns as it lands, so its appearance changes as the viewer moves around it. The monument stood in a fountain basin above the sanctuary's theatre, so the prow seemed to sail through water.

The head and arms are lost. A right hand found on Samothrace in 1950 shows the hand was open, raised in greeting rather than holding a trumpet or wreath. The monument probably celebrated a naval victory, perhaps by Rhodes, but which one is uncertain.

Assembled from over a hundred fragments, it has stood since 1884 at the top of the Louvre's Daru staircase.

name: The Venus de Milo

claims.text: The statue was found on Melos in 1820 and acquired by France.
An inscribed base attributing it to a Hellenistic sculptor was recorded and subsequently lost.
It dates to the late 2nd century BC rather than the Classical period.
The figure originally held an apple.
The base was suppressed deliberately to support a Classical attribution.

milestones.text: Found by a farmer, Yorgos Kentrotas, in a niche among ancient ruins on Melos.
Presented to King Louis XVIII, who gives it to the Louvre.

summary: A Hellenistic Aphrodite found by a farmer on Melos in 1820 — famous partly for what it is missing.
significance: One of the most famous statues in the world, and an example of how later taste reshaped the image of Greek art.
body:
A marble statue of Aphrodite (Venus to the Romans), just over 2 m tall, made around 130–100 BC. A farmer, Yorgos Kentrotas, found it in 1820 in a niche among ancient ruins on the island of Melos. French officers acquired it, it was presented to King Louis XVIII, and he gave it to the Louvre, Paris, where it has been since 1821.

The goddess stands with her weight on one leg, her body twisting in a spiral, nude to the hips with drapery slipping down. Both arms are lost and have never been found. The most likely reconstruction has her holding an apple — *mēlon* in Greek, a pun on Melos and a reference to the apple Paris awarded Aphrodite as the most beautiful goddess.

A base found with the statue named its sculptor as [Alex]andros of Antioch on the Maeander, dating it to the Hellenistic period. The base was later lost. The Louvre had just returned the famous Medici Venus to Italy after the Napoleonic wars and promoted its new statue as a work of the Classical golden age; whether the base was lost by chance or set aside to support that story is unresolved.

Its pose deliberately echoes 4th-century Classical sculpture, which helped the misattribution stick.

name: The Pergamon Altar

claims.text: The Gigantomachy frieze runs approximately 113 m with around a hundred figures.
Figures are carved to break out of the architectural frame onto the steps.
The altar was removed to Berlin in the 1880s.
The frieze allegorises Attalid victories over the Galatians.
A smaller interior frieze depicts the life of the mythical hero Telephus, legendary founder of Pergamon.

milestones.text: Carl Humann excavates the altar and its frieze slabs and ships them to Berlin.
Reconstructed in the newly opened Pergamonmuseum.

summary: A monumental altar whose 113 m frieze shows gods fighting giants in violent high relief — the defining work of Hellenistic baroque.
significance: The defining monument of Hellenistic "baroque" sculpture, and the centrepiece of one of the world's great museums.
body:
A monumental altar built on the acropolis of Pergamon, in western Asia Minor, by the Attalid kings around 170–159 BC, probably under Eumenes II. Carl Humann excavated it in 1878–86 and shipped the sculptures to Berlin under an agreement with the Ottoman government. It was reconstructed in the Pergamonmuseum, Berlin, which opened in 1930.

The altar stood on a high platform with a broad staircase. Around the platform ran a frieze 113 m long and over 2 m high showing the Gigantomachy, the battle of the Olympian gods against the giants. About a hundred figures fight in deep relief: faces twisted in pain, muscles strained, a giant pulled back by his hair as a dog bites into him. Figures spill out of the frame onto the steps, so visitors climb into the battle. A smaller frieze inside tells the story of Telephus, the mythical founder of Pergamon, whom the Attalids claimed as an ancestor.

The emotional intensity is the opposite of Classical restraint. The battle of gods against monsters was understood as an image of the Attalids' own victories over the Galatians (Celts) — order against chaos, with the kings as the gods.

Turkey has long sought the altar's return.

name: The Dying Gaul

claims.text: The Dying Gaul is a Roman marble copy of a Hellenistic bronze from Pergamon.
It formed part of a monument commemorating Attalid victories over the Galatians.
Ethnographic details such as the torc and hair match ancient descriptions of Celts.
The sculptor worked from direct observation of Celtic warriors.

milestones.text: Recorded in the Ludovisi collection after turning up during building work for the Villa Ludovisi.
Taken to Paris by Napoleon's forces; returned to the Capitoline Museums in 1816.

summary: A defeated Celtic warrior dying on his shield — a monument by the victors that treats the enemy with dignity.
significance: A victory monument that gives the defeated enemy full dignity — one of the most moving images of death to survive from antiquity.
body:
A marble statue of a dying Celtic warrior, life-size, a Roman copy of a bronze original made at Pergamon around 230–220 BC. The copy came to light in Rome in the early 17th century and is recorded in the Ludovisi collection by 1623. It is now in the Capitoline Museums, Rome.

The original belonged to a group of statues dedicated by King Attalus I of Pergamon after his victories over the Galatians, Celtic invaders who had settled in central Anatolia. The warrior sits on his fallen shield beside a broken trumpet, propped on one weakening arm, bleeding from a wound in his side, head bowed. His spiky, lime-stiffened hair, moustache and the torc (neck ring) at his throat match ancient descriptions of Celts.

Although it is a monument to victory, it shows the defeated enemy with strength and dignity, his death a private, quiet moment. There is calculation in this — a formidable enemy made the Attalids' victory greater — but the result is one of the most humane images of ancient art.

Napoleon's forces took it to Paris in 1797; it returned to Rome in 1816. Admired by Grand Tour travellers, it was one of the most copied ancient sculptures in Europe.

name: Laocoön and His Sons

claims.text: The group was discovered in Rome in 1506 and identified with a work described by Pliny.
It significantly influenced Michelangelo and later Baroque sculpture.
The original right arm was rediscovered in 1906 and reattached, correcting an 18th-century restoration.
It is a Greek original rather than a Roman copy.

milestones.text: Dug up in a vineyard and identified at once as the work Pliny praised; bought by Pope Julius II.
Ludwig Pollak finds the bent right arm in a builder's yard; it is reattached in the 1950s.

summary: A Trojan priest and his sons killed by sea serpents — unearthed in 1506, and immediately decisive for Renaissance art.
significance: The ancient sculpture that most shaped Renaissance art, and the starting point of a famous modern debate about what images and words can each express.
body:
A marble group, about 2.1 m tall, showing the Trojan priest Laocoön and his two sons attacked by sea serpents. It is dated between about 50 BC and AD 50 and attributed to three sculptors from Rhodes — Hagesander, Athenodoros and Polydoros — whom Pliny the Elder names as the makers of such a group in the palace of the emperor Titus. It was dug up in a vineyard in Rome in 1506, bought by Pope Julius II, and is now in the Vatican Museums.

In the story, Laocoön warned the Trojans not to bring the wooden horse into their city, and was destroyed with his sons by serpents sent by the gods. The sculpture shows the moment of agony: the father strains against the coils, his body twisting, face contorted, while his sons struggle beside him. Whether it is a Greek original or a Roman-period version of an earlier Hellenistic bronze is debated.

Michelangelo saw it on the day it was unearthed, and its straining, twisting bodies fed into his work and into Baroque sculpture. The missing right arm was restored reaching heroically upward; in 1906 the archaeologist Ludwig Pollak found the original arm, bent back towards the head, which was reattached in the 1950s.

In 1766 the critic Lessing used the group in his *Laocoön*, an essay on the different limits of painting and poetry.

name: The Rosetta Stone

claims.text: The stone records a priestly decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek.
It was found by French forces in 1799 and transferred to Britain in 1801.
Champollion used it to demonstrate that hieroglyphs are a mixed phonetic and semantic system in 1822.
Knowledge of Coptic was essential to the decipherment.
The stone is a copy of a decree also issued at other Egyptian temples, so it was not a unique document even in antiquity.

milestones.text: Found by French soldiers rebuilding a fort.
Taken by the British under the Capitulation of Alexandria.
Jean-François Champollion uses it to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.

summary: A Ptolemaic decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek — the key that unlocked ancient Egyptian.
significance: The key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, and a vivid record of Greek kings ruling Egypt through its native priesthood.
body:
A slab of granodiorite about 1.1 m tall, inscribed in 196 BC with a decree of the Egyptian priests meeting at Memphis in honour of the young king Ptolemy V. French soldiers found it in 1799 near the town of Rosetta (Rashid) in the Nile Delta; under the terms of the French surrender at Alexandria in 1801 it passed to Britain, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

The same decree is written three times: in hieroglyphs, the sacred script of temples; in Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script; and in Greek, the language of the Ptolemaic kings and their government. That mix is itself a picture of Hellenistic Egypt, where a Macedonian Greek dynasty ruled an Egyptian population with the support of the native priesthood. Copies of the decree were set up in temples across the country; fragments of others have been found.

Because the Greek could be read, the stone offered a way into the other two scripts. Thomas Young showed that oval cartouches spelled royal names by sound. In 1822 Jean-François Champollion demonstrated that hieroglyphs combine sound signs and meaning signs, and that the language behind them was an earlier form of Coptic, which he knew.

Egypt has asked for the stone's return; the British Museum has declined.

name: Cleopatra tetradrachm

claims.text: Cleopatra VII's coin portraits show pronounced, non-idealised facial features.
Joint issues depict Cleopatra and Mark Antony together.
Plutarch attributes her influence to presence and intelligence rather than beauty.
The coin portraits deliberately assert dynastic authority rather than attractiveness.

summary: Coins struck by Cleopatra VII showing a hook-nosed, sharp-chinned ruler — nothing like the later legend of her beauty.
significance: The only portraits of Cleopatra made in her lifetime with her own approval — and they look nothing like the legend.
body:
Silver coins issued by Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler of Egypt, between 51 and 30 BC, struck at Alexandria and at other mints, including Ascalon and Antioch. Examples are in the British Museum and many other collections.

Her coin portraits show a strong hooked nose, a prominent chin, a firm mouth and large eyes, with her hair tied back in a bun and a royal diadem. They closely resemble the coin portraits of earlier Ptolemaic queens. The effect is of a ruler asserting her place in a long dynasty, not of a beauty: on money, looking like a legitimate monarch mattered more than looking attractive. Plutarch, writing more than a century later, says much the same — that her beauty was not in itself remarkable, but her presence, voice and conversation were irresistible.

Some coins struck in the eastern Mediterranean show Cleopatra on one side and Mark Antony on the other, their profiles cut in a similar style, advertising their political partnership against Octavian.

The later image of Cleopatra as a dangerous seductress comes largely from Roman propaganda after her defeat at Actium in 31 BC, and from later drama and film, not from the evidence of her own coins.

name: The Derveni Krater

claims.text: The Derveni Krater is a bronze volute krater over 90 cm tall and weighing more than 40 kg, found in 1962 in a Macedonian tomb near Thessaloniki.
It was used as an ash urn for the cremated remains of a Macedonian nobleman and a noblewoman.
Its relief frieze depicts Dionysus among maenads and satyrs, and is considered among the finest surviving examples of large-scale Greek bronze metalwork.
An inscription names Astion of Larissa, in Thessaly, as an early owner.

milestones.text: Found during road building in a cist tomb, in the same group of graves that held the Derveni Papyrus.

summary: A colossal bronze wine-mixing vessel from a Macedonian tomb, its cast and hammered reliefs of Dionysus and his followers ranked among the finest surviving Greek metalwork.
significance: It shows a level of technical mastery in large-scale bronze casting and relief work that few other surviving objects can match, and demonstrates the wealth flowing through Macedonian aristocratic circles in Alexander's own generation.
body:
Found by chance in 1962 during road construction near Derveni, north of Thessaloniki, the krater was already an heirloom by the time it was buried: an inscription identifies an earlier owner from Larissa in Thessaly, decades before it ended up holding the ashes of a Macedonian noble couple in their tomb. At over 90 cm tall and weighing more than 40 kilograms of bronze, it dwarfs the everyday grave goods buried alongside it.

Its decoration is exceptional even by the standards of the period: a running frieze in high relief shows Dionysus seated among an ecstatic company of maenads and satyrs, cast and worked with an anatomical fluency that has led some scholars to associate the workshop, speculatively, with major sculptural traditions of the fourth century BC. Smaller figures — animals, further Dionysiac attendants — decorate the neck and volutes.

It was recovered from the same cluster of tombs, and the same 1962 excavation, that produced the carbonised Derveni Papyrus — an accidental double discovery that makes the Derveni tombs one of the richest single archaeological finds from the Macedonian world of Alexander's own lifetime.

name: The Derveni Papyrus

claims.text: The Derveni Papyrus, found carbonised on a funeral pyre near Thessaloniki in 1962, is the oldest surviving manuscript in Europe.
It preserves a philosophical commentary on an Orphic poem about the birth of the gods.
The commentary reinterprets the Orphic poem's mythological content in physical and cosmological terms resembling Presocratic natural philosophy, especially ideas associated with Anaxagoras.
The underlying Orphic poem it quotes may be considerably older than the commentary itself, possibly from the late sixth century BC.

milestones.text: Carbonised remains of the scroll are found on a funeral pyre beside a tomb, the oldest surviving Greek book.
The first full official edition is published.

summary: A carbonised papyrus roll from a Macedonian tomb, the oldest surviving manuscript in Europe, preserving a philosophical commentary on the origin of the gods.
significance: It is a uniquely direct physical link to fifth- and fourth-century BC Greek intellectual life, showing an otherwise-unknown effort to reconcile traditional religious poetry with the new natural philosophy of the Presocratics, rather than treating the two as opposed.
body:
Preserved only because it was accidentally carbonised — turned to a fragile, ash-like char — on a funeral pyre rather than destroyed outright, the Derveni Papyrus survived where ordinary papyrus from this period never does, making it, remarkably, the oldest surviving book in the European archaeological record, older by over a century than the next-oldest comparable find.

Its text is a line-by-line commentary on an Orphic poem describing the birth and succession of the gods, of the same broad tradition as Hesiod's Theogony. Rather than reading the poem as straightforward myth, the commentator interprets it allegorically, treating the gods as symbolic descriptions of physical processes and elements — an approach that draws heavily on the vocabulary and ideas of Presocratic natural philosophy, particularly the cosmology associated with Anaxagoras, in which Mind (nous) organises primordial matter.

The scroll was found among grave goods in the same 1962 excavation near Derveni that produced the Derveni Krater, in a tomb dated to the last third of the fourth century BC — though the commentary's author and the poem it quotes may both be considerably older, opening a rare window onto how Presocratic ideas about nature were already being used to reread traditional religious poetry well before Plato and Aristotle.

name: The Paphos Baetyl of Aphrodite

claims.text: The cult image of Aphrodite at Palaepaphos was not an anthropomorphic statue but a black conical stone, a baetyl.
Ancient authors, including Tacitus, explicitly describe the goddess's image at Paphos as aniconic, rising cone-shaped from a broad base.
The baetyl is depicted within its shrine on Roman-period Cypriot coinage, flanked by attendants.
Aniconic betyl worship at Paphos most likely reflects Levantine and Near Eastern religious tradition rather than a native Aegean Greek one.

summary: The black conical stone worshipped as Aphrodite at her Paphos sanctuary, an aniconic cult image with no human features at all.
significance: It shows that even Aphrodite's most famous Greek sanctuary had, at its ritual core, an image with nothing Greek or anthropomorphic about it -- a reminder that Greek religion absorbed and reinterpreted much older Cypriot and Near Eastern cult practice rather than inventing everything itself.
body:
Visitors expecting a statue of the goddess found something stranger: a smooth, dark, roughly conical stone standing on a base, with no carved face, limbs or drapery. Tacitus, describing the sanctuary in his account of Titus's visit in AD 69, found it notable enough to record in detail -- "the image of the goddess is not in human form... it is a rounded mass, broader at the base and rising like a turning-post to a small circumference" -- evidently as puzzled by it as any other Roman visitor would have been.

The stone's cult standing long outlasted any single building phase of the sanctuary: it appears on Roman provincial coinage from Cyprus, shown standing within a shrine flanked by attendants, centuries after the sanctuary's Late Bronze Age origins. That continuity, across a site rebuilt and administered by Cypriot kings, Ptolemies and Roman governors in turn, suggests the stone itself -- not any particular temple structure around it -- was the real, unbroken object of the cult.

Aniconic stone worship of this kind has closer parallels in Levantine and Near Eastern religion than in mainland Greek practice, fitting Cyprus's position as a cultural crossroads between the Aegean and the Near East. The Paphos baetyl is usually cited as the clearest surviving case of it within the Greek-speaking world, precisely because Greek and Roman visitors kept describing how unlike a normal cult statue it was.

name: The Artemision Bronze

claims.text: The Artemision Bronze is an original Greek bronze of a striding god, slightly over life-size, cast around 460 BC.
It was recovered in two pieces, in 1926 and 1928, from a shipwreck off Cape Artemision at the northern tip of Euboea.
Scholars disagree whether the figure represents Zeus hurling a thunderbolt or Poseidon hurling a trident, since the weapon itself was never found.
The wreck that carried it appears to have been transporting older Greek statuary as cargo, plundered or purchased, centuries after the bronze was made.

milestones.text: Sponge divers recover the first pieces from an ancient wreck.
The head and body are raised, and the statue is assembled.

summary: A striding god caught mid-throw, one of the very few large Greek bronzes to survive as an original rather than a Roman copy, pulled from a shipwreck off Euboea in two pieces decades apart.
significance: Alongside the Riace Bronzes, it is direct physical evidence for what Classical Greek bronze casting actually looked like, rather than what marble copyists later approximated -- and its identity is still argued over precisely because the one detail that would settle it, the object once held in the missing hand, never surfaced.
body:
Sponge divers found the first fragments off Cape Artemision in 1926; further pieces, including the head and torso, came up only in 1928, meaning the statue was assembled from a delayed, two-stage recovery of the same wreck. It shows a bearded god at the height of a throw, weight fully back on the right leg, left arm extended for aim, right arm cocked behind the shoulder -- a pose of total, coiled control rather than strain.

Whatever he once held in his right hand is gone, and with it the surest way to name him. A thunderbolt would make him Zeus; a trident would make him Poseidon. Both readings have serious defenders, and the debate itself is a useful reminder of how much meaning in Greek sculpture depended on now-missing attributes rather than the pose alone.

The wreck that carried it seems to date centuries after the statue's own casting, suggesting it was old cargo -- part of the same current of looted or purchased Greek art moving toward Italy that later swept up the Riace Bronzes -- rather than a contemporary shipment. Both wrecks preserve, by accident, exactly the kind of large-scale original bronze that peacetime Greek and Roman recycling otherwise destroyed almost without exception.

name: The Aphrodite of Knidos
material: Marble original (lost); Roman marble copies survive
museum: No original survives; copies in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere

claims.text: Praxiteles carved the Aphrodite of Knidos in marble around 360-330 BC as a cult statue for the city of Knidos.
It was the first monumental Greek cult statue to show a goddess fully nude, breaking the convention that divine female images be draped.
A circular shrine at Knidos was built to let visitors view the statue from every side, an unusual arrangement for a cult image.
The original does not survive; its appearance is reconstructed from Roman marble copies and ancient written descriptions.

summary: Praxiteles' nude Aphrodite, the first monumental Greek cult statue to show a goddess fully undraped, and by ancient reputation the single most admired statue anywhere.
significance: It reset what a Greek cult image of a goddess was allowed to look like, and its lost original was famous and imitated for centuries after -- a rare case where a work's later reputation is better attested than the work itself.
body:
Ancient tradition, reported by Pliny the Elder, holds that Praxiteles carved two versions of Aphrodite and let the buyer choose: one modestly draped, one fully nude. The people of Kos, offered first pick, took the draped statue as the safer, more traditional option; Knidos took the one Kos had turned down. Whatever the anecdote's exact accuracy, the outcome was real: Knidos ended up with the more radical work, and it made the small city a pilgrimage destination.

The statue showed Aphrodite apparently caught undressing for a ritual bath, one hand loosely shielding her body rather than concealing it, her clothing draped over a nearby vessel. A circular shrine at Knidos was arranged so she could be seen from all sides -- pointedly unlike the frontal viewing typical of temple cult statues, and itself a sign of how much the statue's physical presence, not just its religious function, mattered to viewers.

No original survives. What is known of it comes from Roman marble copies of varying quality (the best-known called the Venus Colonna), coins from Knidos that show its pose, and ancient authors who describe travelling to see it and record Praxiteles' own reported preference for it above all his other work. Its influence outlasted the statue itself by centuries, shaping essentially every later reclining or bathing Aphrodite in Greek and Roman art.

name: The Nike of Paionios

claims.text: The Nike of Paionios was carved around 425-421 BC and set on a triangular pedestal roughly nine metres tall at Olympia.
An inscription on the base records that it was dedicated by the Messenians and Naupactians and signed by the sculptor Paionios of Mende.
The dedication most likely commemorates the Messenian and Naupactian role in the Athenian victory over Sparta at Sphacteria in 425 BC.
The figure was originally winged, shown as if just alighting in flight, with drapery carved to suggest it being pressed back by wind.

milestones.text: Found fallen in front of its pedestal in the first season of the German excavations at Olympia.

summary: A marble Nike shown mid-descent, wind pressing her drapery against her body, set on a nine-metre pedestal at Olympia by the sculptor Paionios of Mende.
significance: Its base inscription makes it one of the few major Classical Greek statues that can be securely dated, attributed to a named sculptor, and tied to a specific historical event, rather than reconstructed from Roman copies and guesswork.
body:
Visitors to Olympia would have seen the statue from a striking distance below: the pedestal alone stood nearly nine metres, putting Nike far above eye level, apparently just touching down after flight. Only her torso and part of the drapery survive intact, but enough remains to show wind-blown cloth clinging to and pulling away from the body in the same figure -- a technical display as much as a religious dedication.

The base inscription is unusually informative. It names the dedicators, the Messenians and Naupactians, and the sculptor, Paionios of Mende, who is otherwise attested as the sculptor of pedimental figures at Olympia's Temple of Zeus. Scholars connect the dedication to the Athenian-allied capture of the Spartan garrison on Sphacteria in 425 BC during the Peloponnesian War, in which Messenian and Naupactian troops served alongside Athens -- though the inscription itself does not name the battle, and the link rests on the coincidence of date and the two cities' known involvement.

Its display at Olympia, a Panhellenic sanctuary shared by all Greeks including Sparta, made the dedication a pointed public statement: a monument to a Spartan defeat, standing permanently within Sparta's own religious world.

name: The Kritios Boy

claims.text: The Kritios Boy, a marble youth of around 480 BC, is the earliest surviving Greek sculpture to use true contrapposto.
Its torso was found in 1865-66 and its head in 1888, in separate excavations south of the Acropolis.
It was recovered from the rubble the Athenians used to level and rebuild the Acropolis after the Persian sack of 480/479 BC, meaning the statue itself must predate that destruction.
The name "Kritios Boy" is a modern attribution based on stylistic resemblance to the documented sculptor Kritios, not a signed or ancient association.

milestones.text: The torso is found in excavations on the Acropolis.
The head is found, and the two are joined.

summary: A marble youth from around 480 BC, the first Greek statue with true contrapposto, buried by the Athenians themselves in the rubble left by the Persian sack of the Acropolis.
significance: It marks, more precisely than almost any other single object, the physical joint between Archaic and Classical Greek sculpture -- and the fact that it was buried as building rubble, not destroyed, is itself a direct trace of the Persian Wars.
body:
Archaic kouroi stand rigidly frontal, weight distributed evenly on both legs, faces fixed in the stylised "Archaic smile". The Kritios Boy breaks that formula: his weight rests on his left leg, his right knee bends and trails, and his hips, torso and head all shift very slightly out of alignment in response -- the first Greek sculpture to render a standing body the way a body actually stands. The face, correspondingly, drops the Archaic smile for a calm, almost severe expression, a shift art historians label the "Severe Style".

Its torso and head were recovered decades apart, in 1865-66 and 1888, in excavations on the Acropolis's south slope -- a separation that itself reflects how the statue survived. It had been broken up and buried, along with a great deal of other sculpture, in the fill the Athenians used to rebuild and level the Acropolis after the Persians burned it in 480/479 BC. That burial, rather than destruction of the stone itself, is why the statue survives at all, and it gives it an unusually secure upper date limit: whatever it depicts, it was carved before the sack that buried it.

The attribution to the sculptor Kritios rests entirely on stylistic comparison with other works associated with him, not on any inscription or ancient text naming this specific statue -- a reminder that even a securely dated, well-preserved piece like this one can still carry an entirely modern name.

name: The Terme Boxer
museum: Museo Nazionale Romano, Palazzo Massimo alle Terme, Rome

claims.text: The Terme Boxer, also called the Boxer at Rest, is a bronze statue of a seated, battered boxer cast sometime between the late 4th and 2nd centuries BC; its exact date and attribution remain debated.
It was found in 1885 during excavations on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, roughly 5.5 metres below ground level.
Its facial wounds, broken nose and swollen ears are rendered in specific anatomical detail, with copper inlays simulating fresh blood and bruising.
It is one of only a small number of large-scale original Greek bronzes to survive, rather than being known solely through later Roman marble copies.

milestones.text: Found by workers digging foundations for a theatre, carefully placed as if deliberately buried.

summary: A bronze boxer shown battered and resting after a bout, one of the few large original Greek bronzes to survive at all, dug up on Rome's Quirinal Hill in 1885.
significance: Greek sculpture turning away from victorious youth to a battered professional resting after a fight — and one of the very few large Greek bronzes to survive at all, so that shift can be read in an original rather than a Roman marble copy.
body:
Workers clearing ground on the Quirinal Hill for a planned theatre in March 1885 struck bronze several metres below the surface. What they had found was a life-size seated boxer, still wearing the leather thongs boxers bound around their hands and forearms, his head turned as if someone had just spoken to him. The scholar overseeing the dig, Rodolfo Lanciani, recognised immediately that this was no ordinary find.

The figure is not an idealised athlete but a specific, damaged body: a broken nose, cauliflower ears, and facial wounds picked out with inlaid copper to suggest fresh blood and bruising under strain and exhaustion. It is exactly the kind of unsparing, individualised realism associated with Hellenistic sculpture's break from Classical idealism, though scholars have argued for dates anywhere from the late 4th to the 2nd century BC and disagree on which historical boxer, if any, it represents.

Its depth below ground and careful positioning have led some to suggest it was deliberately buried in antiquity, perhaps to protect it during a period of unrest, rather than simply lost or discarded. Whatever the reason, that burial is exactly why it survived: alongside the Riace Bronzes and the Artemision Bronze, it is one of the vanishingly rare large Greek bronzes that escaped being melted down for scrap.

name: The Colossus of Rhodes

claims.text: The Colossus was a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, about 33 m tall, made by Chares of Lindos.
It was funded from the sale of siege equipment abandoned by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 304 BC.
It collapsed in an earthquake around 226 BC, after standing some 54 years.
It stood astride the harbour entrance.

relations.rel: paid for by the siege of

summary: A giant bronze statue of the sun god Helios set up at Rhodes around 280 BC — one of the Seven Wonders, which stood for only 54 years.
significance: The most famous of the lost Wonders, a symbol of Hellenistic ambition and engineering, and the origin of the word "colossal".
body:
After Rhodes survived the year-long siege of Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305–304 BC, the Rhodians sold the siege engines he had left behind and used the money to build a thank-offering to their patron god, Helios, the Sun. The sculptor Chares of Lindos, a pupil of Lysippos, spent about twelve years on it, finishing around 280 BC.

The statue was about 33 m tall, roughly the height of the Statue of Liberty from its feet to its crown. It was built of bronze plates over an internal framework of iron bars, weighted with stone, on a marble base. Its exact pose and location are unknown. The popular image of a giant standing astride the harbour mouth, with ships passing between its legs, is a later invention: a statue that size could not have been built that way, and it probably stood near the harbour or on the acropolis.

Around 226 BC an earthquake broke it at the knees and it fell. The Rhodians, citing an oracle, did not rebuild it. Its huge fragments lay where they fell for some eight centuries; Pliny says few people could get their arms around its thumb. In AD 654 Arab forces raiding Rhodes reportedly sold the bronze for scrap.

It was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and its name gave us the word "colossal".

name: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia
material: Gold and ivory over a wooden core

claims.text: Pheidias made the statue for the Temple of Zeus at Olympia in the 430s BC.
The seated figure was about 12 m tall and made of gold and ivory.
Pheidias' workshop at Olympia has been excavated, with moulds and tools for the statue.
It was destroyed in a fire at Constantinople in the 5th century AD.

milestones.text: German excavators identify Pheidias' workshop at Olympia, with clay moulds for the statue's drapery and a cup inscribed "I belong to Pheidias".

summary: Pheidias' colossal seated statue of Zeus in gold and ivory, made for the god's temple at Olympia — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
significance: The most admired cult statue of antiquity, said to have changed how people imagined the king of the gods.
body:
After completing the Athena Parthenos in Athens, the sculptor Pheidias went to Olympia, where in the 430s BC he made the cult statue for the new Temple of Zeus. Zeus sat on an elaborate throne of cedar inlaid with ebony, ivory, gold and precious stones, holding a figure of Victory in his right hand and a sceptre topped by an eagle in his left. The figure was about 12 m tall, its flesh of ivory and its robe and hair of gold, built over a wooden framework. It nearly filled the temple: ancient writers joked that if Zeus stood up he would go through the roof.

Pausanias, who saw it in the 2nd century AD, described it in detail, and its image appears on coins of Elis. It was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and ancient writers said that to see it was to forget one's troubles. Keeping the ivory from cracking in Olympia's damp climate required constant care with oil.

The workshop where Pheidias built the statue, just west of the temple, was excavated in the 1950s; it held tools, clay moulds for the gold drapery and a cup inscribed "I belong to Pheidias".

The statue's fate is uncertain. According to later Byzantine sources it was taken to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire in the 5th century AD.

name: The Gortyn law code

claims.text: The Gortyn code is the longest surviving Greek legal inscription, carved in twelve columns.
It is written boustrophedon, alternating direction line by line.
It deals mainly with family law, property, inheritance and the status of slaves.

milestones.text: Federico Halbherr finds most of the inscription in a mill channel, built into a later Roman building.

summary: The longest Greek law code to survive, inscribed on stone at Gortyn in Crete in the 5th century BC.
significance: A unique first-hand record of Greek law in practice, especially on marriage, inheritance and slavery.
body:
The Gortyn code was carved around 480–450 BC on the curved wall of a public building at Gortyn, a leading city of central Crete. In the Roman period the blocks were reused in a later building, the Odeion, where they survive. The Italian archaeologist Federico Halbherr found most of the text in 1884.

The inscription runs to twelve columns and over 600 lines in the local Doric dialect and early Cretan alphabet. It is written *boustrophedon*, "as the ox ploughs": one line runs right to left, the next left to right.

It is not a complete law code but a collection of laws, chiefly on family and property. It sets out rules on marriage and divorce, the property rights of women, inheritance, the marriage of heiresses, adoption, rape and adultery, and debt. It distinguishes carefully between free citizens, serfs and slaves, setting different penalties and rights for each; a woman could own property and keep it on divorce.

Because almost all other Greek law is known only from speeches and later writers, the Gortyn code is precious evidence of how a Greek city actually regulated family life and status. It is still in place at Gortyn.

name: The Serpent Column

claims.text: The Serpent Column was dedicated at Delphi from the spoils of Plataea in 479 BC.
Its coils are inscribed with the names of 31 Greek states that fought the Persians.
Constantine the Great moved it to Constantinople in the 4th century AD.

summary: The bronze victory monument of three entwined snakes dedicated at Delphi after Plataea in 479 BC, now in Istanbul.
significance: The Greeks' own monument to their victory over Persia, listing the states that fought — one of the most important inscriptions of the Classical age.
body:
After the Greek victory over the Persians at Plataea in 479 BC, the allies dedicated a tenth of the spoils to Apollo at Delphi. The monument was a golden tripod bowl raised on a bronze column of three entwined serpents, about 8 m tall, whose heads supported the bowl.

The Spartan commander Pausanias first had an epigram inscribed claiming the victory for himself. The Spartans erased it and instead inscribed on the coils of the serpents the names of the 31 Greek states that had fought, headed by Sparta, Athens and Corinth. Herodotus and Thucydides mention the monument, and the list largely matches their accounts.

The gold bowl was melted down by the Phocians in the Sacred War of the 4th century BC. In the 4th century AD the emperor Constantine moved the bronze column to his new capital, Constantinople, and set it up in the Hippodrome, where it still stands in what is now Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul. The serpents' heads broke off around 1700; part of one head is in the Istanbul Archaeological Museums.

About 5.5 m of the column survives, with its inscription still legible.

name: Exekias' amphora of Achilles and Ajax

claims.text: The amphora is signed by Exekias as both potter and painter.
It shows Achilles and Ajax playing a board game, a scene not found in surviving literature.
It is regarded as a masterpiece of Athenian black-figure painting.

milestones.text: Found in an Etruscan tomb at Vulci and acquired for the papal collections.

summary: A black-figure amphora of about 540–530 BC, signed by Exekias, showing Achilles and Ajax playing a board game at Troy.
significance: The masterpiece of Athens' greatest black-figure painter — a quiet moment of war, full of tension.
body:
Exekias was the greatest Athenian painter of black-figure pottery, active around 545–525 BC, and also a potter; he signed this amphora as both maker and painter. It was found in an Etruscan tomb at Vulci in Italy and is now in the Vatican Museums.

On its main side, the heroes Achilles and Ajax sit facing each other on blocks, bent over a gaming board during a lull in the fighting at Troy, their spears over their shoulders and shields propped behind them. Inscriptions give their names and their calls: Achilles says "four", Ajax "three". Achilles, still wearing his helmet, is the stronger player.

The scene is not in Homer or any surviving poem, and may be Exekias' own invention. Its power lies in its stillness and concentration: the two greatest Greek warriors absorbed in a game, while the war waits around them. Later readers have seen foreboding in it — both heroes will die at Troy.

Exekias' work shows black-figure painting at its height: figures picked out in fine incised detail, with patterned cloaks and armour drawn with astonishing precision. Within a few years, Athenian painters began to adopt the new red-figure technique, and the scene of the board game was copied many times.

name: The Uluburun shipwreck
material: Cargo of copper, tin, glass, gold and other goods

claims.text: The ship sank off southern Turkey around 1300 BC.
Its cargo included about ten tonnes of copper ingots and one tonne of tin.
Goods aboard came from at least seven cultures, including Cyprus, Egypt, the Levant and Mycenaean Greece.

milestones.text: A sponge diver reports strange metal 'biscuits' with ears — copper ingots.
The Institute of Nautical Archaeology excavates the wreck in over 22,000 dives.

summary: A merchant ship that sank off southern Turkey around 1300 BC, its cargo the richest record of Late Bronze Age trade ever found.
significance: A time capsule of the interconnected Bronze Age world, showing the long-distance trade on which the Mycenaean palaces depended.
body:
In 1982 a Turkish sponge diver reported seeing metal "biscuits with ears" on the seabed off Uluburun, near Kaş on the south coast of Turkey. They were copper ingots from a ship that had sunk around 1300 BC. From 1984 to 1994 the Institute of Nautical Archaeology excavated the wreck at depths of 44–61 m, in over 22,000 dives.

The ship was about 15 m long, built of cedar. Its cargo was extraordinary: about ten tonnes of copper in some 350 ingots, mostly from Cyprus, and a tonne of tin — the right proportion to make bronze; ingots of blue glass; ebony and ivory; ostrich eggs; amber from the Baltic; resin, spices and wine in Canaanite jars; Cypriot pottery; gold and silver jewellery, including a gold scarab of the Egyptian queen Nefertiti; weapons; and a folding wooden writing tablet. Goods came from at least seven cultures, including Mycenaean Greece.

The ship was probably sailing west from the Levant or Cyprus towards the Aegean, perhaps carrying a royal shipment. Its cargo shows the scale of the exchange of raw materials and luxury goods that linked the palace states of Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus, Anatolia and Mycenaean Greece — the world that collapsed a century later.

The finds are displayed in the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology.

name: The Athena Parthenos
material: Gold and ivory over a wooden core
museum: Lost; Roman copies in Athens and elsewhere

claims.text: Pheidias' statue of Athena Parthenos was dedicated in the Parthenon in 438 BC.
It stood about 12 m tall, with over a tonne of gold in its removable drapery.
The original is lost; its appearance is known from small Roman copies such as the Varvakeion Athena.

summary: Pheidias' colossal gold-and-ivory statue of Athena inside the Parthenon, dedicated in 438 BC and now lost.
significance: The centrepiece of Periclean Athens and its treasury in gold, known today only through copies.
body:
The Athena Parthenos was the great cult statue of the Parthenon, made by Pheidias and dedicated in 438 BC. The goddess stood about 12 m tall, in a long robe, wearing a helmet and the aegis, with a figure of Victory (Nike) in her outstretched right hand and her left resting on a shield, with a great snake beside her. Her skin was ivory and her clothing gold, over a wooden core.

The statue was also a reserve of wealth: Thucydides records that its gold weighed 40 talents, more than a tonne, and was removable, so that the city could use it in an emergency, provided it was replaced. Its shield, sandals and base were carved with scenes of battles against Amazons, giants and centaurs, and the birth of Pandora. A legend said Pheidias put portraits of himself and Pericles in the shield's Amazon battle, and was prosecuted for it.

The statue was damaged by fire and repaired in antiquity, and was probably taken to Constantinople in late antiquity; its fate is unknown. Pausanias described it in the 2nd century AD. Its appearance is known from small Roman marble copies, above all the Varvakeion Athena in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens, and from coins and gems.

A full-size modern replica stands in the Parthenon replica at Nashville, Tennessee.

name: The Moschophoros

claims.text: The Moschophoros shows a man carrying a calf as an offering to Athena.
Its base names the dedicator, Rhombos (or Kombos).
It was found in 1864 in the Persian debris on the Acropolis.

milestones.text: Found on the Acropolis in the debris buried after the Persian sack of 480 BC.

summary: An Archaic marble statue of a bearded man carrying a calf on his shoulders, dedicated on the Acropolis around 570–560 BC.
significance: A vivid early image of Greek sacrifice and piety, and one of the masterpieces of Archaic Athenian sculpture.
body:
The Moschophoros ("calf-bearer") is a marble statue made in Athens around 570–560 BC and dedicated on the Acropolis. It was found in 1864 in the debris the Athenians buried after the Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC, and is now in the Acropolis Museum.

A bearded man, wearing a thin cloak, carries a calf across his shoulders, holding its legs in front of his chest. The man's arms and the calf's legs form an X, binding the two together, and the man looks out with the faint "Archaic smile". His eyes were once inlaid with coloured stone. He is bringing the calf to Athena as a sacrifice, a scene repeated in Greek religion for centuries.

The inscription on its base records that it was dedicated by a man whose name was probably Rhombos or Kombos, perhaps the man portrayed. It was carved from Hymettian marble, one of the earliest uses of Attic marble for large sculpture.

The statue is one of the finest works of early Athenian sculpture, combining the stiff frontality of the Archaic style with a tender relationship between man and animal. Its image of a man carrying an animal later shaped early Christian images of the Good Shepherd.

name: Kleobis and Biton

claims.text: The pair of kouroi were dedicated at Delphi by the Argives in the early 6th century BC.
Herodotus tells how Solon named Kleobis and Biton among the happiest of men.
Their identification with Kleobis and Biton rather than the Dioscuri is debated.

milestones.text: Found by the French School's excavation at Delphi.

summary: A pair of massive Archaic marble youths dedicated at Delphi by the Argives around 580 BC, identified with the brothers of a story told by Herodotus.
significance: Among the earliest monumental kouroi, linked to one of Herodotus' most famous tales about human happiness.
body:
Kleobis and Biton are two marble statues of naked young men (*kouroi*), about 2 m tall, dedicated at Delphi around 590–580 BC. They were found in 1893–94 during the French excavation of the sanctuary and are now in the Delphi Archaeological Museum. Heavy and powerful, with large heads, thick limbs and the left foot forward, they are among the earliest monumental kouroi of mainland Greece. An inscription names the Argive sculptor, perhaps Polymedes.

They are usually identified with the brothers in a story told by Herodotus. When Croesus of Lydia asked Solon who was the happiest man he had known, Solon named, second, two young men of Argos, Kleobis and Biton. When the oxen did not arrive to draw their mother, a priestess of Hera, to the goddess's festival, the brothers yoked themselves to the cart and pulled her 45 stades to the temple. She prayed that Hera grant them the best gift for mortals. That night they fell asleep in the temple and never woke. The Argives set up statues of them at Delphi.

Some scholars think the inscription instead refers to the divine twins Castor and Pollux. Either way, the statues show the confident, monumental style of early Archaic Greek sculpture.

name: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus

claims.text: The statue was found in the Temple of Hera at Olympia in 1877, where Pausanias saw a Hermes by Praxiteles.
Whether it is an original by Praxiteles or a later work is debated.
It shows Hermes holding the infant Dionysus, whom he carried to the nymphs.

milestones.text: German excavators find it in the Temple of Hera at Olympia, where Pausanias had described it.

summary: A marble statue of the god Hermes holding the baby Dionysus, found at Olympia in 1877 and attributed to Praxiteles.
significance: Possibly the only surviving original by one of the greatest Greek sculptors — and the classic example of 4th-century grace and softness.
body:
In 1877 German excavators at Olympia found a marble statue of Hermes lying in the Temple of Hera, exactly where Pausanias had seen "a Hermes of stone carrying the infant Dionysus, a work of Praxiteles" in the 2nd century AD. It is now in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia.

The god stands with his weight on one leg in a relaxed S-curve, leaning on a tree trunk over which his cloak is draped. On his left arm he holds the infant Dionysus, whom, in myth, he is carrying to be raised by the nymphs; his missing right hand probably held up a bunch of grapes, teasing the child. The marble is finely polished to suggest soft flesh, and the face is dreamy and gentle.

If by Praxiteles, made around 340–330 BC, it would be the only surviving original by one of the most famous Greek sculptors, whose other works, such as the Aphrodite of Knidos, are known only from copies. But some scholars argue that details of its carving, the back and the support point to a Hellenistic or Roman work, perhaps by a later sculptor named Praxiteles or a copy. The debate is unresolved.

Whoever made it, the statue is the finest surviving example of the graceful, relaxed style of 4th-century BC sculpture, very different from the grandeur of the Parthenon.

name: The Grave Stele of Hegeso

claims.text: The stele marked the grave of Hegeso, daughter of Proxenos, in the Kerameikos cemetery.
It shows Hegeso seated, choosing jewellery from a box held by a servant.
It was found in the Kerameikos in 1870.

milestones.text: Found in the Kerameikos cemetery, Athens, still standing beside the Street of Tombs.

summary: An Athenian grave relief of about 410–400 BC showing the dead woman Hegeso choosing a necklace from a jewellery box held by her maid.
significance: The most celebrated Classical grave relief, a quiet image of a woman's life and death in the style of the Parthenon sculptors.
body:
The grave stele of Hegeso was carved in Athens around 410–400 BC and stood over her grave in the Kerameikos, the city's main cemetery outside the Dipylon Gate. It was found there in 1870 and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens; a copy stands on the original spot.

The relief, framed like a small shrine with pillars and a pediment, shows Hegeso, identified by the inscription as "Hegeso, daughter of Proxenos", seated on an elegant chair with her feet on a footstool. She lifts an item of jewellery — once painted, probably a necklace — from a box held open by a young servant girl standing before her. Both look down at it in silence.

The scene is not the moment of death but an image of the dead woman as she was in life, absorbed in an everyday act within the household. Her rich clothes and the jewellery show her family's wealth and her role as a well-born Athenian wife, the servant reminds us of the enslaved women in such households, and the calm, gentle mood is typical of Athenian grave reliefs, which avoided showing grief openly.

The figures' soft drapery and serene faces closely resemble the Parthenon sculptures, and the relief may come from a workshop trained on them. Thousands of such stelae were made in Athens until a law of around 317 BC banned luxurious grave monuments.

name: The Parian Marble
museum: Ashmolean Museum, Oxford; Paros Archaeological Museum

claims.text: The Parian Marble is a Greek chronicle inscribed on Paros in 264/3 BC.
It lists dated events from the legendary king Cecrops of Athens to 299/8 BC.
Most of the upper part is in the Ashmolean Museum, having been brought to England in the 1620s.

milestones.text: Agents of the Earl of Arundel acquire the upper part in Smyrna and bring it to London.
Given to the University of Oxford; now in the Ashmolean Museum.
A further fragment is found on Paros, now in the Paros museum.

summary: A marble chronicle inscribed on the island of Paros in 264/3 BC, listing the dates of events in Greek history from mythical times.
significance: The oldest surviving Greek chronological table, showing how Greeks themselves dated their past — myth and history alike.
body:
The Parian Marble (*Marmor Parium*) is a chronicle carved on a marble slab on the island of Paros in the Cyclades in 264/3 BC. Its author is unknown. It survives in pieces: the upper part was bought in Smyrna in 1627 for the Earl of Arundel and taken to London, where part was lost in the Civil War, and given to Oxford University in 1667; it is now in the Ashmolean Museum. A further fragment was found on Paros in 1897.

The inscription lists events from the reign of Cecrops, the legendary first king of Athens, dated by the Greeks to 1581 BC in our terms, down to 299/8 BC, counting each as so many years before 264/3 BC. It dates both what we would call myth and history: the flood of Deucalion, the arrival of Cadmus, the fall of Troy (1209/8 BC by its reckoning), the first Olympiad, the lives of poets such as Homer, Hesiod and Sappho, the battles of Marathon and Salamis, the deaths of Socrates and Alexander.

Its dates are mostly given by Athenian archons, and it shows a particular interest in poets, music and festivals. Some of its dates differ from those of other ancient chronographers, such as Eratosthenes.

The Parian Marble is invaluable evidence for ancient Greek chronology and for how Greeks constructed a single timeline out of legend and recorded history.

name: The Canopus Decree

milestones.text: Karl Richard Lepsius finds a complete copy at Tanis

claims.text: The decree was passed by an assembly of Egyptian priests at Canopus in 238 BC in honour of Ptolemy III and Berenice II.
It introduced a leap day every four years into the Egyptian calendar, a reform that did not last.
Its well-preserved trilingual text confirmed Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs.

summary: A priestly decree of 238 BC in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, honouring Ptolemy III and Berenice II and reforming the calendar.
significance: A fuller trilingual text than the Rosetta Stone, it confirmed the decipherment of hieroglyphs and records an early attempt at a leap year.
body:
In March 238 BC the priests of Egypt met in synod at Canopus, near Alexandria, and passed a decree honouring Ptolemy III and Queen Berenice II for their gifts to the temples, the return of sacred statues carried off by the Persians, and their relief of a famine with imported grain. They established a new class of priests in their honour and deified their young daughter Berenice, who had just died.

The decree also reformed the calendar. The Egyptian year of 365 days slipped against the seasons by a day every four years; the priests ordered an extra day every fourth year — the idea behind the leap year. The reform was not kept, and it was the Romans under Augustus who made a leap year last in Egypt.

Like the Rosetta Stone, the decree was inscribed on stone in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek and set up in temples. In 1866 the German Egyptologist Karl Richard Lepsius found a complete copy at Tanis in the Delta, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo; other copies have been found since. Its long, nearly undamaged texts confirmed that Champollion's method of reading hieroglyphs, worked out from the Rosetta Stone, was correct.

name: The Zenon archive
museum: Dispersed: Cairo, London, Florence, Ann Arbor and other collections

milestones.text: Local diggers uncover the archive at Philadelphia in the Fayum; it is sold off and dispersed

claims.text: The archive of about 2,000 papyri belonged to Zenon of Kaunos, manager of a large estate in the Fayum.
The estate, of about 10,000 arouras, was a gift of Ptolemy II to his finance minister Apollonius.
It is the largest surviving archive from Ptolemaic Egypt.

summary: About 2,000 Greek papyri of the 3rd century BC from the files of Zenon, manager of a great estate in the Fayum under Ptolemy II.
significance: The richest window onto daily life and government in Ptolemaic Egypt.
body:
Zenon was a Greek from Kaunos in Caria who worked for Apollonius, the *dioikētēs* or finance minister of Ptolemy II. Ptolemy gave Apollonius a huge estate of about 10,000 arouras (some 2,750 hectares) of reclaimed land at Philadelphia, a new town in the Fayum, the fertile basin west of the Nile. From about 256 BC Zenon ran it.

He kept his papers, and around 1914–15 local diggers found them at Philadelphia. The archive was sold off and is now divided among collections in Cairo, London, Florence, the University of Michigan and elsewhere. About 2,000 documents survive, dating from about 261 to 229 BC.

They are letters, accounts, contracts, petitions and memoranda, in Greek, with a few in demotic. They show the estate's vineyards, olive groves and wheat fields, irrigation works and imported Greek crops and livestock; Egyptian farm workers complaining of unpaid wages or striking; officials, tax collectors and travellers; and Zenon's own interests, including his greyhound and the education of young athletes. They reveal the close-run, profit-minded management of Ptolemaic Egypt, and the meeting of Greek settlers and Egyptian villagers.

name: Greek graffiti at Abu Simbel
material: Sandstone (leg of a colossus of Ramesses II)

claims.text: Greek mercenaries in the army of Psammetichus II carved their names on a colossal statue of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel during his Nubian campaign of 591 BC.
They are among the earliest securely dated Greek inscriptions.
The writers came from Ionian and Dorian cities including Teos, Colophon and Ialysos on Rhodes.

summary: Names scratched in 591 BC by Greek mercenaries of the pharaoh Psammetichus II on a colossal statue of Ramesses II, far up the Nile.
significance: Among the earliest dated Greek inscriptions, and vivid evidence of Greeks serving in Egypt three centuries before Alexander.
body:
From the 7th century BC the pharaohs of the 26th Dynasty employed Greek and Carian mercenaries, the "bronze men from the sea" of Herodotus. In 591 BC Psammetichus II sent an army south against the kingdom of Kush in Nubia. On its way, at Abu Simbel, some of his Greek soldiers carved graffiti into the left leg of one of the four colossal seated statues of Ramesses II outside the great temple, already about 650 years old.

The longest inscription reads, in translation: "When King Psammetichus came to Elephantine, this was written by those who sailed with Psammetichus son of Theocles. They came beyond Kerkis, as far as the river allowed. Potasimto led the foreign-speakers and Amasis the Egyptians." It is signed by Archon son of Amoibichos and Pelekos son of Eudamos. Other soldiers added their names and home cities, including Teos, Colophon and Ialysos on Rhodes.

Because the campaign is dated, the graffiti are among the earliest securely dated Greek inscriptions, and they show the forms of letters used by Greeks of different regions. When the temple was moved in the 1960s to save it from the waters of Lake Nasser, the inscribed statue went with it.

name: Fayum mummy portraits
material: Encaustic (wax paint) or tempera on wooden panels
museum: Many collections, including Cairo, the British Museum, the Louvre and Berlin

milestones.text: The dealer Theodor Graf buys a large group of portraits found at er-Rubayat
Flinders Petrie excavates portraits in the Roman cemetery at Hawara

claims.text: About a thousand painted portraits survive from the mummies of Roman Egypt, dating from the early 1st to the mid-3rd century AD.
They were painted on wooden panels and bound over the faces of the mummified dead.
They are the largest surviving body of Greek-tradition panel painting.

summary: Lifelike painted portraits of men, women and children of Roman Egypt, placed over their mummies in the 1st–3rd centuries AD.
significance: The only large group of ancient panel paintings to survive, and the faces of the Greek-Egyptian society of the Roman period.
body:
Greek painters such as Apelles and Zeuxis were the most admired artists of antiquity, but their panel paintings have all perished. The closest we can come to their art is a group of about a thousand portraits from Roman Egypt, found mainly in the cemeteries of the Fayum, the fertile basin west of the Nile, and at other sites such as Antinoopolis.

They were painted on thin wooden panels in hot wax (encaustic) or in tempera, in the Greek naturalistic tradition, and then wrapped into the linen bandages of the mummy so that the face looked out — a fusion of Egyptian burial custom with Greek and Roman portraiture. The sitters, men, women and children, wear Roman hairstyles, jewellery and clothes, and many have Greek names. They were probably descendants of the Greek settlers of the Ptolemaic period who had intermarried with Egyptians. Some portraits may have been painted in life, others at death.

In 1887 the Viennese dealer Theodor Graf acquired many found at er-Rubayat, and in 1887–88 and 1911 Flinders Petrie excavated more at Hawara, recording their contexts. The custom faded in the 3rd century AD.

name: Greek fire
material: Unknown; probably based on crude oil
museum: None survive; known from texts and one manuscript illustration

claims.text: The chronicler Theophanes says Greek fire was invented around 672 by Kallinikos, an architect from Heliopolis in Syria.
It was a liquid incendiary, sprayed from siphons on ships, that burned on water.
Its exact formula was a state secret and is now lost; most scholars think it was based on crude oil.

summary: The secret incendiary weapon of the Byzantine navy, invented around 672, which burned even on water.
significance: It helped save Constantinople from the Arab sieges of the 7th and 8th centuries, and its secret was so well kept that it is still unknown.
body:
According to the chronicler Theophanes, around 672 a refugee architect named Kallinikos, from Heliopolis in Syria, brought the Byzantines a new kind of fire. It was a liquid that was heated and pumped under pressure through bronze tubes (*siphōnes*) mounted in the bows of warships, projecting a stream of flame that stuck to whatever it hit and could not easily be put out with water. Smaller hand-held versions and grenades were also used.

Greek fire was decisive in the great Arab sieges of Constantinople in 674–678 and 717–718, when it destroyed many enemy ships, and it was used later against the Rus' fleets that attacked the city in 941 and 1043. The Byzantines called it "liquid fire" or "sea fire"; "Greek fire" is the name later used by western Europeans.

The recipe was a state secret, known only to a few families, and the emperor Constantine VII warned his son never to reveal it to foreigners. It has been lost. Most historians think it was based on crude oil from the Black Sea region, perhaps mixed with resins, and that the secret lay as much in the pumping apparatus as in the liquid. It seems to have fallen out of use by the time of the Fourth Crusade in 1204.

name: Venetus A

milestones.text: Part of the manuscript collection Cardinal Bessarion gives to Venice
Jean-Baptiste-Gaspard d'Ansse de Villoison publishes its scholia, sparking debate on how the Iliad was composed
The Homer Multitext project publishes high-resolution digital images

claims.text: Venetus A, copied in Constantinople in the 10th century, is the oldest complete manuscript of the Iliad.
Its margins preserve scholia drawn from the work of Alexandrian scholars such as Aristarchus.
Villoison's publication of its scholia in 1788 helped inspire Wolf's theory that the Homeric poems were composed orally.

summary: The oldest complete manuscript of Homer's Iliad, copied in 10th-century Constantinople, with ancient scholarly notes in its margins.
significance: The most important surviving witness to the text of the Iliad and to the work of the Alexandrian scholars who edited it.
body:
Venetus A is a large parchment book of 327 leaves, copied in Constantinople around the middle of the 10th century, a time of renewed interest in classical texts. It contains the whole *Iliad*, with extensive notes (*scholia*) written around the text in smaller script. These notes are excerpts from ancient commentaries, going back to the Alexandrian scholars Zenodotus, Aristophanes of Byzantium and especially Aristarchus, who edited Homer in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC. The manuscript even preserves the critical signs Aristarchus used in the margins to mark lines he doubted.

The manuscript belonged to Cardinal Bessarion, who left his library to Venice in 1468, and it is now in the Biblioteca Marciana as *Marcianus Graecus* Z. 454 (= 822). Its importance was recognised in 1788, when the French scholar Villoison published its scholia. They showed that the ancient text of Homer had varied widely, which helped the German scholar F. A. Wolf argue in 1795 that the Homeric poems were composed orally and written down only later, launching the modern "Homeric Question".

Since 2007 the Homer Multitext project has made complete digital images of it freely available.
